chapters.title: Chapter 351: Camilla’s Reassessment
paragraphs: ’He is concealing far more than he allows others to see,’ Camilla thought as she looked at him.
After all, even she had been deceived. Not by a lie. Not by an illusion. But by the simple assumption that Stan was what he appeared to be.
A New Age human could not possess resources of this caliber. That much was obvious.
The infrastructure required to obtain treasures like these no longer existed on Earth. Entire sects had once gone to war over resources of lesser value.
Yet Stan kept producing them. Again and again. As though such things were ordinary.
Her eyes narrowed slightly. ’No. He cannot be a genuine mortal of this era.’
That explanation creates more questions than answers. The possibilities continued to unfold.
’New Terra? An undiscovered inheritance holder? The hidden disciple of some surviving ancient faction? Someone carrying the legacy of a force that escaped the Night of Vanishing?’
None of the theories fit perfectly. Yet each of them made more sense than the idea that Stan Harrison was simply what he appeared to be.
Her thoughts shifted toward his spatial artifact. The thing disturbed her most.
She had never sensed it activate. Never sensed spatial fluctuations. Never sensed Qi expenditure. Items appeared. Items vanished. Entire volumes of condensed Qi moved from one location to another.
And yet there was nothing. No trace. No signature. No mechanism she could identify.
’Even Royal Blood clans possess spatial artifacts with detectable fluctuations. So what exactly is that thing?’
The question lingered. Then another realization surfaced.
’He also allowed me to place him beneath a blood pact.’
A truly dangerous thought.

’If he were simply a greedy mortal, he would have lied at some point. If he were a fool, he would have revealed something he should not. Yet every answer he has given has survived scrutiny. Every answer has been technically truthful.’

The pieces began to align. Not perfectly. But enough. His strange techniques. His unfamiliar tools. His impossible wealth. His undetectable artifact. His lack of fear. His willingness to hand over treasures without concealment.
Taken individually, each could be dismissed. Taken together, they formed a pattern. The theory settled into her mind with uncomfortable elegance. Not as certainty. But a possibility.
A possibility dangerous enough that it could not be ignored.
’He is hiding something profound.’
Whether it was cultivation, lineage, an inheritance, or something else entirely, she could not yet determine.
But she was no longer willing to assume that Stan was merely an unusually fortunate human.
Her perspective shifted. Until now, she had viewed him with the faintly indulgent amusement of a Royal Blood entertaining an interesting mortal.
That framework quietly collapsed. In its place remained caution. Curiosity.
And a growing sense that she was standing in front of a mystery far larger than she had initially believed.
Stan’s words echoed in her thoughts. ’I look forward to our partnership.’

Camilla met his eyes again. This time with genuine attention. Not as one might regard a mortal. Not as one might regard a curiosity. But as one evaluates an unknown variable whose limits have yet to be discovered.
Then she nodded. A genuine nod. The kind one offered a potential equal.
"Yes," she said quietly. "I look forward to it as well."

Stan noticed the shift. He caught it in her posture, in the subtle sharpening of her attention, and in the specific quality of her nod. Somewhere during the last minute, Camilla had reassessed him. Whatever assumptions she had previously been operating under had been quietly discarded and replaced with something else.
Something that now ranked him considerably higher in her internal evaluation. He wasn’t entirely sure why.
At the moment, he didn’t particularly care. He was a busy man with a broken werewolf to deal with.
Stan filed the observation away for later and turned his attention back to the pack leader sprawled across the polar ice.

The werewolf was still conscious. Still watching them. Still glaring at both of them with the burning hatred of a predator that had finally realized exactly what it had walked into and had yet to accept the lesson.
A familiar chime echoed through Stan’s mind. ’The system.’
[Spending on Camilla Dragomir confirmed.]
[Favorability Tier: 80-89 (8× Rebate).]
[Note: Rebate tier locked at spending initiation.]
[Rebate issued: 683,008 liters of condensed liquid Qi.]
[Deposited into Host Inventory.]

Stan barely reacted. The notification informed him that over six hundred and eighty thousand liters of condensed liquid Qi had just been deposited into his inventory, eight times the amount he had given Camilla.
A treasure vast enough to send ancient sects into open warfare. He dismissed the thought almost immediately.
The Qi wasn’t going anywhere. The werewolf was.
And right now, the werewolf had his full attention.
Stan walked over to the broken pack leader and crouched beside him.

The werewolf remained trapped in his transformed form. The shift-lock Camilla had placed on him earlier was still active, forcing him to remain in the lupine body she had spent the last several minutes creatively dismantling.
His condition was, in every meaningful sense, catastrophic.

Every long bone in his body was fractured. His tail was gone. His Qi reserves had been drained to nearly nothing. His breathing came in shallow, uneven rasps. His physical strength remained formidable. His ability to use it had been completely destroyed.
Stan crouched until they were at eye level. Then he smiled.
"So, dog." His voice carried the quiet satisfaction of a man who had spent several hours looking forward to this exact conversation. "What do you think of the payback?"
The werewolf’s eyes burned with cold fury. Its body could no longer obey it. Its Qi was exhausted. Its bones were shattered. But its hatred remained intact.
Blood dripped from the corner of its mouth as it forced its jaw to move.
"Royal Vampire." The words emerged as a low, ragged growl. "Why are you doing this?"
Its gaze shifted toward Camilla.
"Do you truly believe my race will allow this?"
Camilla remained silent. The werewolf pressed on.
"You suppress me because your bloodline is superior."
A harsh cough interrupted him. Dark blood splattered onto the ice.
"But what about Alpha Bloods?" Its lips peeled back. "Can you treat them the same way?"
Its gaze sharpened as it added coldly; "What will your precious vampire race think when they learn that a Royal Blood has chosen the side of the livestock?"

The polar wind howled across the ice. For a moment, nobody spoke. Then Camilla’s expression cooled. Not dramatically. Not visibly, to most people. But just enough. Enough for Stan to notice. Enough for the werewolf to notice that he had crossed the line.
Camilla looked at him as one might look at something unpleasant stuck to the bottom of a shoe.
"Noisy."
She raised a hand and waved.
A thin line appeared across the werewolf’s throat. For a brief second, nothing happened. Then the line widened. The head slid from the neck.
It struck the ice with a dull thud and rolled several meters before coming to a stop and then silence returned.
Dark blood spread slowly across the white ice, steaming faintly in the Antarctic air.
Camilla lowered her hand; "He was becoming irritating."

chapters.title: Chapter 352: Elder Fang falls
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Stan looked at Camilla.

He was, if he was being honest, a small amount disappointed. He had wanted to be the one to end the werewolf. The pack leader was, in a very specific and personal sense, ’his’ — the being who had dragged Stan’s face across this same polar ice, and had cut open his abdomen, and had spoken to him like meat. Stan had, at some point in the past twelve hours, been quietly looking forward to being the one whose hand ended him.
Camilla caught his gaze.
She looked briefly away.

"What," she said with a small, defensive scoff. "He is still alive. Even with his head cut off, it will take some time for him to actually die. If you want the honor of finishing him, you still can. I was simply... silencing him. He was being loud."
Stan let out a small, dry breath.

He could tell she had done it partly because she had wanted to, and partly because she had not quite been able to stomach hearing the werewolf accuse her, aloud, of siding with what her race had spent centuries considering food.
He didn’t press her on it. He nodded slowly and moved to the werewolf’s body.
He willed both pieces, the massive transformed body and the severed head, into his inventory.

The werewolf’s will, with its head separated from its body and its consciousness already collapsing into the specific dying-brain state that followed decapitation, was too weak to resist the storage. His transformed corpse dematerialized from the polar ice in a heartbeat and settled into Stan’s private storage space alongside the polar bear, the Rift Wolves, the Void Mantis, the Mirror Serpent, the Abyss Bats, and the Void Whale, every trophy Stan had accumulated over the past several hours of impossible days.
The polar ice around them, moments before crimson with blood, was now empty except for the drying stain of what had been left behind.
Stan straightened up.
His system chimed.
[Target Elder Fang: eliminated.]
’So he’s called Elder Fang,’ Stan thought. ’Fitting.’

The notification was, he suspected, delayed because the werewolf had continued to survive in his inventory for a small period after Stan had stored him. The inventory’s lack of ambient oxygen, combined with the werewolf’s decapitated state and his depleted Qi reserves, had presumably accelerated his final death. Within a minute or so of storage, the werewolf had, for all intents and purposes, ceased to exist.
Stan filed that observation away with the small, cold discipline of a man who was starting to build a proper tactical model of what his inventory could and couldn’t do.
The system chimed again.
[Notice: Host has been marked.]
Stan’s expression tightened. ’Marked? The fuck?!’

The specific implications sat immediately in his mind. Werewolves, if their internal lore matched what the Introduction to Earth had described, possessed pack-scent tracking capabilities that operated over considerable distances. If Elder Fang had, in his final moments, applied some kind of aura mark to Stan, some spiritual signature that other werewolves could track, then Stan was going to have a very bad time the next time he encountered another member of the same clan.
He was not, at his current strength, ready to fight a pack led by an alpha.
He was barely ready to fight what he had already fought. His face changed.
He was about to consider what protective measures the system might offer through the shop when the next notification arrived.
[The Mark is being suppressed.]
Stan blinked.
[The Mark has been suppressed.]
Stan let out the long, slow breath of a man whose luck had, for once, held.

The system had apparently registered the mark and had, of its own accord, taken defensive action. Whatever mechanism it had used to suppress the tracking signature was operating quietly in the background, the same infrastructure, Stan suspected, that had been suppressing his financial transaction trails for weeks. Whatever the system was, it had a consistent talent for hiding him from surveillance he did not wish to be subject to.
He would look into the mechanics later. For now, the immediate threat had been contained. He glanced at Camilla.

She was watching him with a small, thoughtful expression, the specific expression of a Royal Blood who had noticed his face change through two separate registers in the span of a few seconds and had drawn her own conclusions about what had happened.
She said nothing. He appreciated the discretion.
He straightened, brushed the polar dust off his coat, and looked out toward the horizon of the endless white plain.
"Alright, Camilla." His voice was calm again. "Let’s get moving. I have a very long trip ahead, and a very long list of people who are going to be extremely upset with me by the time I get home."
She smiled slightly. "Lead the way, human."
He walked forward across the polar ice.
She fell into step beside him. Together, they moved away from the empty Spirit Pool cavity, away from the site of the werewolf’s death, away from every trace of what had just happened here.
Behind them, the polar wind picked up.

They walked in silence for a few minutes, the endless white plain stretching out ahead. Stan was just about to will the plane back into existence when he paused, glanced at Camilla, and asked the question that had been forming in his mind since the werewolf’s death.
"Now that the portal is closed, does that mean the demihumans and True Humans your realm was going to send never actually made it through?"
Camilla was silent for several seconds.

"I’m no expert on portals," she said eventually. "But I do know when one opens a path to an unknown place, those who cross do not choose where they arrive. The portal seeks concentrations of Qi and deposits arrivals nearby."
Her crimson eyes swept across the endless white landscape.
"In the current era of Earth..." she paused. "This place is the only location I have sensed with Qi dense enough to attract a crossing. The Spirit Pool acts as a beacon."
She folded her arms. "If demihumans or True Humans had already entered Earth before the portal closed, they should have appeared somewhere in this region."

chapters.title: Chapter 353: First Contact
paragraphs: Camilla folded her arms. "If the beastkins and True Humans had already entered Earth before the portal closed, they should have appeared somewhere in this region."
She paused for a while...

"But I cannot detect any of them within my sensing range. Which means, most likely, they never made it through. The portal closed before their groups were dispatched. Whatever they had planned to send, they will need to send again, through a different portal, at some point in the future."
"Hmm."

Stan shrugged and let the answer settle in his mind. The realm’s next attempt would presumably require the formation to weaken further. Which meant he had time. How much time, he didn’t yet know, but time.
The stillness of the Antarctic wasteland was broken by a distant rumble.
Camilla noticed it first.

Her head turned. Her red eyes narrowed. She held up a single finger to Stan and tilted her head toward the horizon, listening with the layered attention of a Royal Blood whose senses extended significantly further than his did.
Stan followed her gaze.

Three tracked snow vehicles crested a distant ridge, their treads carving deep grooves into the polar surface as they advanced in coordinated formation toward the Spirit Pool coordinates. Heavy antennas jutted from their roofs. Soldiers were partially concealed behind the armored sides of the transports, weapons visible in the loading ports.
Standing on the open rear platform of the lead vehicle was a figure Stan recognized immediately.
The scientist. Wrapped in thick polar gear, he was scanning the landscape through a pair of high-magnification binoculars, calmly directing the convoy with small hand gestures.

Stan’s system-enhanced vision picked out the face from a distance that would have been impossible for an ordinary human. He knew that face from the news reports. The senior glaciologist who had first announced the discovery of the Spirit Pool.
’Are these people from the government or one of those hidden families?’
He sighed inwardly.

The question was almost rhetorical. Special forces snow transports carrying a coordinated soldier detail and a lead scientist did not, in any recognizable modern framework, belong to a private research consortium. Whatever agency had sent this convoy, it was one that operated with military resources and had decided the Spirit Pool was worth an armed retrieval mission.
Camilla, standing beside him, was picking up more than he was.

The distance was significant, perhaps two kilometers, but her Royal Blood senses extended well beyond ordinary auditory range. She could hear the voices inside the vehicles as clearly as if they had been standing beside her.
"A little east."
"Slow."
"Keep the ridge on your left."
Then, the scientist’s binoculars swept across the plain, and locked.
"Movement."
The convoy slowed immediately.
"I’ve got two individuals.
The scientist adjusted his focus.
"One male. One female."
A pause.
"And blood?" The scientist’s voice, calm until that moment, lost its composure. "There’s a pool of blood staining the snow not too far from them."
The convoy came to a complete stop.
"How did they even get her so fast without these special cars" one of them added
Within moments, the rear ramps of all three vehicles lowered simultaneously.

Special forces soldiers spilled out with the practiced, coordinated efficiency of an elite unit that had rehearsed exactly this deployment. Some fanned out to firing positions behind the vehicles. Others took cover behind natural ice formations. The remaining soldiers stayed inside the transports, their rifles resting against the open firing ports.
Red laser dots bloomed across the snow.
One settled on Stan’s chest.
Another rested squarely between Camilla’s eyes.
More followed as additional marksmen locked onto them from every position along the convoy’s perimeter.
Camilla, unhurried, glanced down at the crimson dot resting on the back of her hand. She smiled faintly.
"What delightful little toys."
Stan’s heart sank.
Laser sights. Military-grade. Communications equipment. Helmet cameras. Almost certainly drones overhead too.

This operation would be documented from beginning to end. Whatever happened in the next few minutes would be recorded, transmitted, archived, and analyzed by an intelligence apparatus that would spend months studying every second of the footage.
A commanding voice echoed across the frozen landscape, amplified by a loudspeaker mounted on the lead vehicle.
"Unknown individuals. You are surrounded. Remain where you are. Raise your hands slowly."
Stan raised his hands.

He did it exactly the way the voice had asked him to do it, slowly, palms open, no sudden motions, the specific compliance posture of a civilian who understood exactly how to avoid being shot by nervous military personnel.
Camilla did not move.
Her smile remained gentle.
The officer continued.
"Step away from each other. Do not attempt to flee. The area is under military control."
The scientist lowered his binoculars slightly, still staring.
"Those are bloodstains behind them, correct?"
He raised the binoculars again and studied Camilla.
"No visible injuries. No weapon."
He shifted his focus to Stan.
"Same with him."
One of the soldiers, positioned behind the lead vehicle, keyed his radio.
"Be careful. Something isn’t right."
The intelligence officer beside the scientist narrowed his eyes.

The scene, from their perspective, defied every explanation his training could produce. A field littered with gigantic wolf carcasses. A calm young man in a heavy coat standing peacefully with his hands raised. A woman with red hair smiling as if she were attending a garden party in the middle of the Antarctic.
An impatient soldier muttered into his radio.
"They’re insane."
Another chuckled.
"Doesn’t matter. If either one twitches, I put them on the ground."
Camilla let out a soft, elegant laugh.
She turned her head slightly toward Stan.
"I haven’t signed your blood contract yet."
Her smile remained warm, almost affectionate, as she said the words.
"So, I assume it’s perfectly acceptable for me to discipline these rude little ants."
Stan’s pupils shrank.

He had recognized the scientist the moment the convoy had crested the ridge. He knew who the man was. He knew what he represented. The Spirit Pool discovery had already gone viral across every major news outlet in the modern world. If any single individual currently alive on Earth was capable of connecting a supernatural event to the world’s governments, of establishing an official, documented, institutional record that the impossible was real and being witnessed by trained personnel, it was this specific scientist standing on the rear platform of the lead vehicle with a pair of binoculars and a satellite uplink.

The stillness of the Antarctic wasteland was broken by a distant rumble.
Camilla noticed it first.
Her head turned.
Her red eyes narrowed.
She held up a single finger to Stan and tilted her head toward the horizon, listening with the layered attention of a Royal Blood whose senses extended significantly further than his did.
Stan followed her gaze.
Three tracked snow vehicles crested a distant ridge, their treads carving deep grooves into the polar surface as they advanced in coordinated formation toward the Spirit Pool coordinates.
Heavy antennas jutted from their roofs.
Soldiers were partially concealed behind the armored sides of the transports, weapons visible in the loading ports.
Standing on the open rear platform of the lead vehicle was a figure Stan recognized immediately.
The scientist.
Wrapped in thick polar gear, he was scanning the landscape through a pair of high-magnification binoculars, calmly directing the convoy with small hand gestures.
Stan’s system-enhanced vision picked out the face from a distance that would have been impossible for an ordinary human.
He knew that face from the news reports.
The senior glaciologist who had first announced the discovery of the Spirit Pool.
’Are these people from the government or one of those hidden families?’
He sighed inwardly.
The question was almost rhetorical.
Special forces snow transports carrying a coordinated soldier detail and a lead scientist did not, in any recognizable modern framework, belong to a private research consortium.
Whatever agency had sent this convoy, it was one that operated with military resources and had decided the Spirit Pool was worth an armed retrieval mission.
Camilla, standing beside him, was picking up more than he was.
The distance was significant, perhaps two kilometers, but her Royal Blood senses extended well beyond ordinary auditory range.
She could hear the voices inside the vehicles as clearly as if they had been standing beside her.
"A little east."
"Slow."
"Keep the ridge on your left."
Then, the scientist’s binoculars swept across the plain, and locked.
"Movement."
The convoy slowed immediately.
"I’ve got two individuals.
The scientist adjusted his focus.
"One male.
One female."
A pause.
"And blood?" The scientist’s voice, calm until that moment, lost its composure.
"There’s a pool of blood staining the snow not too far from them."
The convoy came to a complete stop.
"How did they even get her so fast without these special cars" one of them added
Within moments, the rear ramps of all three vehicles lowered simultaneously.
Special forces soldiers spilled out with the practiced, coordinated efficiency of an elite unit that had rehearsed exactly this deployment.
Some fanned out to firing positions behind the vehicles.
Others took cover behind natural ice formations.
The remaining soldiers stayed inside the transports, their rifles resting against the open firing ports.
Red laser dots bloomed across the snow.
One settled on Stan’s chest.
Another rested squarely between Camilla’s eyes.
More followed as additional marksmen locked onto them from every position along the convoy’s perimeter.
Camilla, unhurried, glanced down at the crimson dot resting on the back of her hand.
She smiled faintly.
"What delightful little toys."
Stan’s heart sank.
Laser sights.
Military-grade.
Communications equipment.
Helmet cameras.
Almost certainly drones overhead too.
This operation would be documented from beginning to end.
Whatever happened in the next few minutes would be recorded, transmitted, archived, and analyzed by an intelligence apparatus that would spend months studying every second of the footage.
A commanding voice echoed across the frozen landscape, amplified by a loudspeaker mounted on the lead vehicle.
"Unknown individuals.
You are surrounded.
Remain where you are.
Raise your hands slowly."
Stan raised his hands.

He did it exactly the way the voice had asked him to do it, slowly, palms open, no sudden motions, the specific compliance posture of a civilian who understood exactly how to avoid being shot by nervous military personnel.
Camilla did not move.
Her smile remained gentle.
The officer continued.
"Step away from each other.
Do not attempt to flee.
The area is under military control."
The scientist lowered his binoculars slightly, still staring.
"Those are bloodstains behind them, correct?"
He raised the binoculars again and studied Camilla.
"No visible injuries.
No weapon."
He shifted his focus to Stan.
"Same with him."
One of the soldiers, positioned behind the lead vehicle, keyed his radio.
"Be careful.
Something isn’t right."
The intelligence officer beside the scientist narrowed his eyes.
The scene, from their perspective, defied every explanation his training could produce.
A field littered with gigantic wolf carcasses.
A calm young man in a heavy coat standing peacefully with his hands raised.
A woman with red hair smiling as if she were attending a garden party in the middle of the Antarctic.
An impatient soldier muttered into his radio.
"They’re insane."
Another chuckled.
"Doesn’t matter.
If either one twitches, I put them on the ground."
Camilla let out a soft, elegant laugh.
She turned her head slightly toward Stan.
"I haven’t signed your blood contract yet."
Her smile remained warm, almost affectionate, as she said the words.
"So, I assume it’s perfectly acceptable for me to discipline these rude little ants."
Stan’s pupils shrank.
He had recognized the scientist the moment the convoy had crested the ridge.
He knew who the man was.
He knew what he represented.
The Spirit Pool discovery had already gone viral across every major news outlet in the modern world.

If any single individual currently alive on Earth was capable of connecting a supernatural event to the world’s governments, of establishing an official, documented, institutional record that the impossible was real and being witnessed by trained personnel, it was this specific scientist standing on the rear platform of the lead vehicle with a pair of binoculars and a satellite uplink.

chapters.title: Chapter 354: Too Late
paragraphs: Stan had recognized the scientist the moment the convoy had crested the ridge. He knew who the man was. He knew what he represented.
If Camilla killed him, the entire modern order was going to shift.

Not because a single scientist mattered by himself. Because the scientist’s death, on video, transmitted live to whatever intelligence infrastructure was monitoring this convoy, would confirm every conspiracy theory that had ever been quietly whispered about Antarctica. It would confirm the existence of supernatural beings.

It would confirm the existence of powers that could kill trained soldiers without visible effort. It would confirm, in the specific way that only documented military footage could confirm, that the world had crossed into a new register of reality.
The consequences of that confirmation would be immediate and enormous.

Every major government would mobilize. Every major military would begin preparing for supernatural threats. Every ordinary human on Earth would learn, within days, that vampires and werewolves and things worse than either had returned.
Stan wanted humanity to have more time.

He wanted the transition to be gradual. Controlled. Guided by his own judgment and his own resources rather than by the panic response of an entire species that had just discovered its historical foundations were wrong.
He opened his mouth. "Camilla, don’t..."
But it was too late, she was gone.

The polar air where Camilla had been standing was suddenly empty. Stan’s system-enhanced senses caught only the faintest ripple of displaced air in her wake, a small, thin fracture in the substance of the space between them and the convoy, healing itself within a heartbeat.
He didn’t see her cross the distance. He saw the result.
The lead vehicle’s rear platform.

The scientist was mid-sentence into his radio when Camilla materialized directly behind him. His mouth was open on a word he would never finish. The binoculars were still raised to his eyes. His breath still fogged the polar air before him.

Camilla appeared beside him with the fluid instantaneity of a Royal Blood who had, evidently, decided that Stan’s "don’t" was a request rather than an order and that a request could be considered after the fact.
She swept her hand and an invisible Qi-blade traced a line across the platform.

The two soldiers flanking the scientist collapsed sideways in the same instant. Their bodies fell in perfectly synchronized angles, their heads separating cleanly from their necks, tumbling to the metal deck with two small hollow thuds. The scientist did not have time to register the sound.
He turned his head. His eyes met Camilla’s.
For a fraction of a second, his mind failed to comprehend how a red-haired woman could be standing where, only an instant ago, there had been no one at all.
Then Camilla’s hand moved.

The Qi-blade sliced across his throat with the same effortless precision she had used on Elder Fang. The scientist’s body swayed for one long moment before the strength left it. He collapsed backward against the platform’s railing and slumped to the deck beside his binoculars.
His pool of blood was small. Neat. Almost apologetic.
The soldiers behind the vehicles opened fire.

Two of them had somehow spotted her arrival, a testament to the reflexes of highly trained specialists drilled to fire at the first sign of an anomaly. Their rifles cracked through the polar air. Muzzle flashes bloomed in short, bright bursts against the snow.
Camilla turned her head. She smiled.

Not because she needed to, she had slowed deliberately. Stan understood, as he watched, that she had reduced her speed to a mere fraction of what it had been a moment earlier, just fast enough to evade the incoming rounds. She was curious. She wanted to see what these little modern toys could actually do.
The bullets, to her senses, moved with agonizing slowness. She stepped sideways observing them with curiosity and intrigued.

The first round passed through empty air where her shoulder had been. She tilted her head three centimeters to the left. The second round passed above her ear. She raised a single finger and let the third bullet strike the tip of it, the small metal projectile compressing against the pad of her fingernail with a soft tink before dropping to the snow, deformed and harmless.
She examined the flattened round for a heartbeat.

’Interesting.’ Her mind cataloged the properties. ’A small kinetic delivery system. High velocity. Low mass. Modern humans have compressed their combat capability into these tiny projectiles. Their strength as individuals is negligible, but the tools are creative. A lesser cultivator would struggle to counter them.’
She raised her eyes to the shooters.

She was still standing on the lead vehicle’s platform. The nearest soldier was thirty meters away, behind the middle transport, firing on full automatic in a panicked spray that his training had, apparently, momentarily failed him.

She waved her hand. Multiple invisible Qi-blades zipped outward across the polar air, following individual trajectory paths that Stan’s senses could barely track. The blades reached the soldiers before the soldiers had registered that she had moved. Heads separated from bodies in a rippling cascade. Rifles clattered to the snow. Boots crumpled beneath their owners.
The convoy’s radio channels erupted into confused shouting.
The remaining soldiers inside the transports began firing through the loading ports.
Camilla vanished from the platform. She reappeared inside the middle transport. The screaming lasted perhaps two seconds.
She reappeared inside the third transport. The screaming there lasted less.

She materialized back on the polar ice a heartbeat later, standing exactly where she had been standing before the entire sequence had begun. Her red hair drifted in the polar wind. Her expression carried the small, contained pleasure of a Royal Blood who had thoroughly enjoyed a demonstration.
Fifteen soldiers. One scientist. One driver.
All dead.
The three snow transports sat in the polar wind with their engines still idling, their armored sides pockmarked with bullet holes from the panicked interior fire, their loading ramps still open.
The polar wind carried the faint, wet smell of blood across the ice.

Stan stood very still. He had barely tracked her movements. He had caught the first blur toward the platform, the momentary slowdown around the shooters, the second blur toward the middle transport. Everything else had happened in gaps his perception could not fill.
He had not stopped her. He looked at the convoy.

At the scientist’s body slumped against the platform railing. At the young soldier’s boots still pointed skyward from behind the lead vehicle. At the loading ramp of the third transport, from which a single hand extended limply into the snow.
The polar wind stirred the fabric of the scientist’s polar jacket.
Stan’s chest felt strange.

chapters.title: Chapter 355: The First Line: Don’t Means Don’t
paragraphs: The polar wind stirred the fabric of the scientist’s polar jacket.
Stan’s chest felt strange upon seeing this...

He had, in his life, seen violent death before. He had caused violent death in the past twenty-four hours. He had watched a Royal Blood torture a werewolf pack leader with something close to enjoyment less than an hour earlier.
This was different.

The scientist had not been armed. He had been holding binoculars. His voice, over the loudspeaker, had ordered his soldiers to detain, not to fire. The soldiers had fired only after Camilla had begun killing them. They had been doing their jobs. They had been ordinary human beings employed by a government that had sent them into the field to investigate an anomaly.
They were not the Red Serpents. They were not the werewolves. They had not consented to this.
The Void Sovereign’s words from a few hours earlier surfaced in Stan’s mind with unwelcome clarity. ’I want your word that you will draw the line under the worst of what would otherwise happen.’
He had drawn no line.
He had said ’Camilla, don’t’ and she had ignored him and he had done nothing else.
His hands felt cold inside his gloves.
Camilla lifted her hand.
She examined the tip of her index finger. A single small droplet of blood clung to it, a trace from some part of the past few seconds that had reached her skin.
She brought the finger to her mouth.
She licked it, slowly, the way a woman who had been on a long fast might taste the first thing offered to her. Her eyes half-closed. The polar wind caught the edge of her hair.
Then she opened her eyes and smiled.
She turned toward Stan who was giving her a shocked, dumbfounded gaze...
"What?" Her voice was warm. Almost teasing.

Stan didn’t answer. He looked at her for a long moment. His face did not carry the expression she had, apparently, expected to find there. There was no fascination on it. There was no shocked awe. There was no flicker of the complicated attraction that a Royal Blood was, evidently, accustomed to producing in beings of every species she encountered.
There was only a slow, hard cold. His voice, when it came, was flat; "Camilla."
She tilted her head. Her smile faded by a small, careful fraction.
"You killed the scientist.
"Yes."
"He wasn’t a threat."
"He was a witness."
"His men were following his orders. He ordered them to detain us. Not to fire."
"They fired anyway."
"After you started killing them."
Camilla was quiet, then she said, "They’re nothing more than annoying insects. It’s what they deserve for daring to speak to me like that..."

The polar wind moved between them. Her expression, which had been comfortably indulgent a moment earlier, began to shift into something more attentive. She was, for the first time in their acquaintance, actually studying his face rather than treating it as a source of amusement.
She was, evidently, reading something in his expression that she had not expected to find.
Stan kept speaking. His voice remained level. He did not raise it.
"I said don’t."
"You did?"
"Yes I did, but you did it anyway."
"Oh."
"Why?"
Camilla considered.

She could have deflected. She could have offered the practical justification, that the scientist was the single most dangerous witness in the modern world, that his continued existence would have triggered exactly the institutional cascade Stan had feared, that killing him now was cleaner than killing him later. All of that was true. All of it was, on some level, defensible.

She chose to be honest instead. "I have lived a very long time, human. In my world, people like these are not to be spared. They are to be removed. Their removal is not personal. It is procedural. Things like this always comes back to bite one later on if not handled correctly."
She paused. "I did not think you would object as strongly as you are objecting."
Stan let out a slow, controlled breath. "You didn’t think about it at all."
"That’s true."
"Camilla."
"Yes."
"When I say don’t, you don’t.
She held his eye.
Her expression, for the first time since he had met her, was neither amused, indulgent, nor teasing. It was quiet. Measured.

The specific quiet of a Royal Blood who was, apparently, processing a piece of feedback from a person she had recently accepted as her comrade and who had just realized that comrade was, in some way she had not fully appreciated, holding her to a standard she had not consciously agreed to.
"Understood." She said it plainly. "I will not do it again."

Stan did not thank her. He walked past her without another word and moved toward the nearest vehicle. He needed to see the scientist’s body properly. He needed to look at what had just been done in his presence, on his behalf, by a woman who was, thanks to a binding he had personally applied to her, bound to his interests.
The scientist was slumped against the platform railing.
Stan stood over him for a long moment.

The man had been in his late fifties. His polar jacket was still zipped correctly. His binoculars were still hanging by their strap from one gloved hand. His expression, in death, carried the small, faintly puzzled look of a person who had not, in the last second of his life, been given enough time to fully understand what was happening to him.
Stan crouched beside him. He closed the scientist’s eyes with two gentle fingers.
He stayed there for a moment. Then he stood up. He turned back toward Camilla.
"We have work to do."
His voice was still level. Whatever he was feeling had been pushed down beneath the practical necessity of what the next several hours were going to require.

"You probably don’t know what those are but They’re are almost certainly satellites monitoring this convoy. There is almost certainly a control center receiving the transports’ telemetry in real time. There are almost certainly drones somewhere overhead. Their sensors are going to have registered every second of what just happened. If those recordings reach the outside world, every government on Earth will know that supernatural beings are real, within twenty-four hours."

He looked at her. "I need you to help me clean this up. Every camera. Every radio. Every hard drive on every vehicle. Every drone in the air, if there are any. All of it. And I need you to help me make sure no signal made it out."
"Like just destroy any thing you think is a ’new age toy’..."
Camilla nodded once. "Understood."

"And Camilla." She waited. "The next time I tell you not to do something, you don’t. Regardless of your reasoning. Regardless of your instinct. Regardless of what your world would have done. You defer to me. That’s the terms of our comradeship from now on."
"...Yes, Stan." She had never, at any point in their acquaintance, called him by his given name.
He nodded once, tightly, and turned toward the transports. There was a great deal of work to do.
The Antarctic wind picked up around them, and the polar dusk began, at last, to deepen toward night.

chapters.title: Chapter 356: The Crimson Blur
paragraphs: Looking at him, Camilla smiled to herself.

’No matter how good your acting is, cultivator, you cannot hide from me that you are a high cultivator in disguise. Only a cultivator of considerable standing would care so much about mortal witnesses. Only a strategist would consider the political consequences of a scientist’s death this quickly. You are protecting an entire species from a truth that will disrupt them, and only someone very powerful would think in those terms.’
She kept the thought off her face.
She flashed him a small, unhurried smile.
"There are about three strange toys hovering high above us. Once I’ve destroyed them, I will clear this region of all these strange toys, as you asked."
Stan nodded once and she moved.
Her feet left the ice.

She rose into the polar sky in a single unhurried lift, her body ascending through the atmosphere with the smooth, effortless authority of a Royal Blood in her element. The three drones were suspended perhaps two kilometers up, small, silver-white shapes, holding position in a triangulated formation designed to maintain constant surveillance of the Spirit Pool site.
They did not detect her approach until she was among them.
Her hand swept once.
The first drone came apart in the sky.

Not exploded. Not shattered but diced, its polymer chassis, its optical sensors, its rotor assemblies, its internal communication modules, all of it sliced simultaneously into hundreds of small, uniform fragments that hung in the air for a heartbeat before beginning to fall.

The Qi-blade patterns Camilla had woven through it had passed through every critical component at once, in a lattice too complex for any modern analytical technology to reverse-engineer from the wreckage.
The second drone met the same fate a heartbeat later. The third followed.

By the time the first drone’s fragments hit the snow, all three had already been reduced to unrecoverable debris. Whatever their sensors had captured in the seconds before their destruction would remain sealed inside components too fragmented to be reconstructed.
Camilla descended.
Her feet touched the ice a hundred meters from where Stan was still standing beside the convoy. She smoothed her hair with one delicate hand.
"That should do for the ones directly above."
Stan nodded slowly. He had watched her rise and return. His face was still carrying the same quiet, hard expression it had worn since the convoy. He did not smile at her.
She noticed but said nothing.
She turned toward the horizon and vanished again.
In a windowless control room somewhere along the Antarctic coast, a soldier stared at his terminal in silence.
Three red icons on his tactical display had, in the past ten seconds, gone dark.
He watched them for a long moment.
Then he brought his palm down on the desk with the flat, controlled crack of a man forcing himself not to shout.
"The drones are gone."
The senior officer across the room, a lean, greying man in his early fifties whose posture carried the accumulated weight of a career in special operations, did not raise his voice.
"I can see that."

"But sir. Look at the last frames." The soldier pulled up the drone feeds’ final captured seconds and threw them onto the wall display. Three separate camera perspectives ran in parallel. Snow. Sky. Snow. Sky. A vague, blurred shape in one of the frames that could have been a bird. Then static.

The soldier gestured. "That’s it. That’s everything they captured. No target lock. No thermal signature. No visual identification. Nothing that any modern analysis suite could turn into an intelligence product."
The senior officer stared at the wall display.

Behind him, another junior officer had brought up the convoy’s telemetry feeds on a second wall panel. All three vehicles were still transmitting basic diagnostic data, engines idling, systems nominal, transponders live. None of the crew’s biometric monitors were transmitting.
Every soldier on the mission was, by every measurable indicator, dead.
The scientist’s biometric monitor had gone flat two minutes earlier.
The senior officer let out a long, slow breath.
"What are we dealing with."
He did not phrase it as a question. It was, in the specific way that questions became statements when a person had finally accepted the shape of the situation, a resigned observation.
The junior officer at the drone console kept talking.

"We recovered fragmented audio from the convoy’s onboard recording before the systems went down. Two individuals. One male. One female. English-language exchange in the seconds before the encounter. The male said ’Camilla, don’t.’ The female didn’t respond audibly before."
He stopped.
"Before what."
"Before every biometric on the convoy flatlined. All within the same two-second window."
The room was silent.
The senior officer walked to the wall display and stared at the static frame that represented the last thing the drone cameras had captured.

"How does a two-person unarmed contact eliminate a fifteen-soldier detail plus a civilian scientist and a driver in two seconds. On camera. With drone coverage. With satellite oversight. And not leave a single frame of usable footage.
The soldier at the console did not answer. Neither did the junior officer.
The senior officer closed his eyes for a long moment.
"Are the Families in on this?"

"...Possibly, sir. Their movement in the past forty-eight hours suggests they know something. Some of them arrived at the peninsula two days ago and haven’t moved since. They’re waiting for something."
"Or someone."
"Yes, sir."
The senior officer opened his eyes. "We need countermeasures."
"Against what, sir? We don’t know what it is. We don’t have visual identification. We don’t have movement data. We don’t have."
"I know what we don’t have." The senior officer’s voice was still level. "Which is why I’m telling you we need countermeasures. Start working on the problem. Every asset we can spare."
The room began to move. He was about to add another instruction when a technician at the far end of the room called out.
"Sir."
His voice was tight.
"Sir. We have another contact."
The senior officer turned.
"What."
"Something is approaching the base at high-speed. Unclassified."
The senior officer’s face did not change.
He had already, on some deep operational level, understood that this was about to happen the moment the drones had gone dark.
He walked to the technician’s console.
He looked at the display.
The tactical map showed a single unclassified contact moving toward the base at a velocity his brain found hard to process.
"Sound the general alarm!"

chapters.title: Chapter 357: Beyond Detection
paragraphs: "Sound the general alarm!"
He said it with gritted teeth. "Full defensive posture. All personnel to stations."
The klaxons began to wail across the base.
[WARNING!]
[WARNING!!]
[UNKNOWN HIGH-SPEED OBJECT DETECTED.]
[ATTEMPTING TARGET LOCK. FAILED.]
[ATTEMPTING THERMAL LOCK. FAILED.] [ATTEMPTING VISUAL CONFIRMATION. FAILED.]

The klaxons rang through the corridors of the base. Personnel scrambled to defensive positions. Emergency shutters descended over the exterior windows. The auto-turrets on the perimeter walls swiveled to face the direction of the incoming contact.
Inside the operations room, the senior officer stood at the central console.
"What’s its speed." The technician was pale. "We can’t calculate it, sir."
"What do you mean you can’t calculate it."

"The system can’t resolve it. Whatever it is, it’s moving faster than our tracking algorithms can process. We’re getting fragmentary signal, the object crosses our detection cone faster than the sensor’s sampling rate. It’s not that we can’t see it. It’s that we can’t see it clearly enough."
"Put it on the cameras."

The tactical wall display switched to the base’s external surveillance feed. Every camera in the outer perimeter fed into the display simultaneously. Fifty-six panels of external footage, each one showing the endless snowstorm of the Antarctic coast.
Every panel showed the same thing. Snow. Wind. Nothing.
"It’s not there."
"It is, sir."
"Where."
"We don’t know."
The senior officer’s jaw tightened.
Another technician’s voice cut across the room. "Sir. Something just passed through Sector Three."
"What."
BOOM!

The base shook. The communications tower, a hundred and twenty meters tall, three hundred meters from the operations center, was suddenly not there. The wall display’s Sector Three feed showed a slow-motion collapse of the entire structure as it fell in on itself, split into hundreds of clean vertical sections, its steel skeleton reduced to falling debris.
Every soldier in the room went silent.
BOOM!
The radar installation.
Gone...
The radar was, when Camilla was finished, a scattering of steel fragments and severed cable trays. Its antenna dishes had been reduced to what looked like carefully quartered orange slices.
BOOM!
The auto-turret battery on the western perimeter.
Gone.
BOOM!
The base’s central satellite uplink array.
Gone.
[WARNING. RADAR SYSTEM FAILURE]
[WARNING. SATELLITE UPLINK LOST]
[WARNING. EMERGENCY POWER GRID DAMAGED]
[WARNING. WEAPONS SYSTEMS OFFLINE.]
The systems shouted their failures into the ears of soldiers who could do nothing about them.
BOOM!
The auxiliary generators.
BOOM!
The eastern perimeter defenses.
BOOM!
Every piece of surveillance equipment attached to the base’s exterior.

The senior officer stood at the console watching every red icon on his tactical display go dark, one by one, in the specific ordered rhythm of a systematic disarmament being conducted by something that knew exactly where his equipment was and exactly how to destroy it.
He did not shout.
He did not issue further orders.
He simply watched.

At one point, one of the high-speed forensic cameras, a piece of equipment normally used for tactical playback of live-fire exercises, captured something after its footage was slowed down by a factor of several hundred.
The frame appeared on the wall display.
For less than a fraction of a second, it showed a beautiful woman with red hair, suspended mid-motion in the polar air, her hand extended in a small, elegant sweeping gesture.
She was smiling, then she was gone.
The room was silent. The senior officer stared at the frame.
"...Was that a human?"
Nobody answered him. The soldier at the console beside him spoke slowly, without lifting his eyes from his terminal.
"No human can move at those speeds, sir."
The senior officer nodded slowly with a heavy heart. He had no idea what the fuck was going on...
Camilla arrived at the base’s central operations center approximately eight minutes after her first pass through the perimeter.

She had, by that point, systematically destroyed every piece of surveillance, communications, weapons, and detection equipment the base carried. She had also, during her rapid patrol of the coastline, destroyed the equivalent equipment maintained by the informal Strange Families settlement that operated under the base’s semi-official protection, every private drone, every family-owned surveillance suite, every satellite ground station, every high-fidelity recording device that could have captured any part of the Antarctic incident.
She left the buildings themselves intact. She left the personnel alive.
She had promised Stan she would not kill any more humans, and she was, as she had told him in the cave, a being of her word.
She materialized in the operations room in a single silent motion.
The soldiers already inside the room raised their sidearms with the immediate, drilled response of trained personnel confronting an intruder.
Camilla looked around.
Her crimson eyes swept the room.

She took in the array of small handguns pointed at her from various angles. She took in the tactical displays showing the base’s now-completely-degraded defensive capability. She took in the senior officer at the central console, who had not raised his sidearm and was, instead, watching her with the specific quiet composure of a man who had accepted that his weapon would not have mattered.
She smiled.
’So much enticing blood,’ she thought. Her tongue traced along her upper lip once, involuntarily.
A trace of reluctance moved across her expression.
’But I promised.’
Her eyes moved once more across the room. Then she vanished.
The wall displays flickered.

Every diagnostic system in the operations center reported that the base was still standing. Every external sensor confirmed that the woman had, once again, exceeded their detection capacity. Every attempt to track her retreat produced null results. She was simply too fast.
The soldiers slowly lowered their weapons.
The senior officer stood at the central console for a long moment.
Then he closed his eyes. He rubbed his temples with two fingers, feeling a headache rise.
"...I need a full incident report drafted."
The junior officer at the drone console straightened up.
"Sir. Yes, sir."

"Everything. Convoy loss. Drone destruction. Base infrastructure. The visual capture from the forensic system. All of it. Flagged priority one, forwarded up the chain the moment we recover our long-range communications. I want it in the hands of national command within twelve hours."
"Yes, sir."
The junior officer paused.
"Sir. What about the Strange Families? They observed the incident from their own settlement. Their equipment was also destroyed. They’re going to have questions."
The senior officer’s expression tightened.

"Let them ask their questions through official channels. Whatever they know or don’t know, this is a national security matter now. It stops being an informal peninsula arrangement the moment a hostile unknown eliminates a full military detail and disables a sovereign facility. I don’t care what the families claim to know. Their intelligence is going through us from here on."
"Understood, sir."

chapters.title: Chapter 358: The Flying Bird
paragraphs: "Their intelligence is going through us from here on."
"Understood, sir."
With that the junior officer turned toward his terminal and began drafting.
The senior officer walked to the wall display, where the last captured frame of the woman, beautiful, red-haired, smiling, mid-gesture, still hung on the panel.
He looked at it for a long moment. Then he pulled up the archive interface and marked the frame for secure preservation. Every fragment of imagery.

Every scrap of sensor data. Every audio recording, however fragmented. All of it was going into the classified vault and, from there, up the chain to whoever at national command was going to be handling the analysis.

He did not delete the recording. He was, in the specific way that career operators were, a man who understood that the correct response to an event this far outside standard operating parameters was to preserve every piece of evidence and let the analysis run wherever it needed to run.
Whatever the woman was, whatever the convoy had encountered, whatever the incident meant, his job was to report it, cleanly and fully, and let the people above him decide what to do.

He turned back to the operations room. "Get me a manual radio relay. Redundant channels. I want a courier plane on standby the moment weather permits. We’re going to be moving hard evidence out of this facility in physical form as well as by uplink. Nothing about this incident lives on this base alone."
The room began to move. Whatever came next, it was going to be for national command to decide.
Back at the Spirit Pool site, Camilla returned to Stan’s side.
She materialized on the polar ice a few paces from him, her hair drifting in the wind, her expression composed. "It’s done."
Stan looked at her.

He had spent the intervening minutes standing in silence beside the convoy. Whatever he had been thinking about, he had not yet resolved. His face still carried the same quiet cold it had worn since she had killed the scientist.
But he nodded once. "Thank you."
She waited. He did not offer more than that.
She accepted the small distance without comment.

The polar wind pushed at their backs. The endless white plain stretched away in every direction, unbroken to the horizon in every direction Stan turned his head. Somewhere in the accumulated exhaustion of the past several hours, the werewolves, the inheritance, the trials, the pact with the Void Sovereign, the beating of Elder Fang, his revenge and all that, Stan’s body was finally beginning to register that it had not slept in what was, by any honest measure... days. In truth, it had been scarcely two days, but so much had happened in that short span of time that it felt far longer. Stan could feel the accumulated exhaustion settling into his bones.
He needed to go home.
Anyways, Camilla looked at him and said, "It’s too bad I don’t get to taste human blood. Anyways, I’m ready to sign your blood contract."
Hearing her, Stan smiled. He had already bought the Blood Contract Technique from the System for 5 System Points and knew what to do.
He summoned a sheet of paper before slicing his thumb with the Fang Dagger. Using his blood, infused with Qi, he wrote down the terms of the contract.
Camilla’s expression turned serious. She manipulated a drop of blood out of her thumb and pressed it onto the paper.
With that, the contract was signed.
The terms were rather unique and somewhat complicated, but she didn’t mind. She felt they were reasonable. More than anything, she wanted to know how long Stan intended to keep his mask on.

Camilla glanced sideways at him and said with a smile. "When dealing with those toys, my senses spread wide and I could see the ocean outside this frost place is bigger than I imagined, how did you get here?"
Stan considered the question. "By plane."
"By what?" She tilted her head. "What is a plane?"
"A flying vehicle. Modern engineering. Fast, large, capable of transcontinental travel."
"You mean a vehicle that can fly like a bird?"
"Something like that. It doesn’t flap. But it flies."
"Interesting." She turned the word over slowly, like she was tasting it. "Interesting.
"You’re curious, aren’t you."
"I have been asleep for a very long time, cultivator. Everything is interesting."
"Fair point."
"And you are going to retrieve it now. This plane."
"That’s the plan."

Camilla laughed, the same low, delighted laugh she had produced when he had explained the same trick to her earlier in the cave. It carried, this time, a slightly different quality. There was more warmth in it. More genuine appreciation. The kind of amusement a person only produced when they had accepted, on some deep level, that they were going to enjoy the company of the person making them laugh for the foreseeable future.
She was filled with curiosity...
Stan didn’t mind her gaze as he willed the plane into existence.

The Bombardier materialized on a stretch of relatively flat, wind-packed snow perhaps fifty meters from where they stood. Its polished fuselage caught the low polar sun in long mirror-bright reflections along its side. Its landing gear settled into the compacted snow with the soft, muted crunch of thirty tons of engineered aircraft finding new solid ground. The whole craft appeared in the polar air with the casual instantaneity that Stan was, slowly, becoming used to.
Camilla did not move for a long moment.

She stared. Her red eyes tracked the length of the fuselage from nose to tail. She catalogued the sweep of the wings. She looked at the twin engines mounted at the rear, the raised T-tail, the small blinking navigation lights at the wingtips that had begun their patient rhythm the instant the aircraft had drawn breath in the real world.
"...This," she said slowly, "is your bird."
"This is my bird."
"It is enormous."
"It’s on the smaller end for its class."
"There is a larger class?"
"Yes, there is a much larger class."

sentences.text: "Their intelligence is going through us from here on."
"Understood, sir."
With that the junior officer turned toward his terminal and began drafting.
The senior officer walked to the wall display, where the last captured frame of the woman, beautiful, red-haired, smiling, mid-gesture, still hung on the panel.
He looked at it for a long moment.
Then he pulled up the archive interface and marked the frame for secure preservation.
Every fragment of imagery.
Every scrap of sensor data.
Every audio recording, however fragmented.
All of it was going into the classified vault and, from there, up the chain to whoever at national command was going to be handling the analysis.
He did not delete the recording.

He was, in the specific way that career operators were, a man who understood that the correct response to an event this far outside standard operating parameters was to preserve every piece of evidence and let the analysis run wherever it needed to run.
Whatever the woman was, whatever the convoy had encountered, whatever the incident meant, his job was to report it, cleanly and fully, and let the people above him decide what to do.
He turned back to the operations room.
"Get me a manual radio relay.
Redundant channels.
I want a courier plane on standby the moment weather permits.
We’re going to be moving hard evidence out of this facility in physical form as well as by uplink.
Nothing about this incident lives on this base alone."
The room began to move.
Whatever came next, it was going to be for national command to decide.
Back at the Spirit Pool site, Camilla returned to Stan’s side.
She materialized on the polar ice a few paces from him, her hair drifting in the wind, her expression composed.
"It’s done."
Stan looked at her.
He had spent the intervening minutes standing in silence beside the convoy.
Whatever he had been thinking about, he had not yet resolved.
His face still carried the same quiet cold it had worn since she had killed the scientist.
But he nodded once.
"Thank you."
She waited.
He did not offer more than that.
She accepted the small distance without comment.
The polar wind pushed at their backs.
The endless white plain stretched away in every direction, unbroken to the horizon in every direction Stan turned his head.

Somewhere in the accumulated exhaustion of the past several hours, the werewolves, the inheritance, the trials, the pact with the Void Sovereign, the beating of Elder Fang, his revenge and all that, Stan’s body was finally beginning to register that it had not slept in what was, by any honest measure... days.
In truth, it had been scarcely two days, but so much had happened in that short span of time that it felt far longer.
Stan could feel the accumulated exhaustion settling into his bones.
He needed to go home.
Anyways, Camilla looked at him and said, "It’s too bad I don’t get to taste human blood.
Anyways, I’m ready to sign your blood contract."
Hearing her, Stan smiled.
He had already bought the Blood Contract Technique from the System for 5 System Points and knew what to do.
He summoned a sheet of paper before slicing his thumb with the Fang Dagger.
Using his blood, infused with Qi, he wrote down the terms of the contract.
Camilla’s expression turned serious.
She manipulated a drop of blood out of her thumb and pressed it onto the paper.
With that, the contract was signed.
The terms were rather unique and somewhat complicated, but she didn’t mind.
She felt they were reasonable.
More than anything, she wanted to know how long Stan intended to keep his mask on.
Camilla glanced sideways at him and said with a smile.
"When dealing with those toys, my senses spread wide and I could see the ocean outside this frost place is bigger than I imagined, how did you get here?"
Stan considered the question.
"By plane."
"By what?" She tilted her head.
"What is a plane?"
"A flying vehicle.
Modern engineering.
Fast, large, capable of transcontinental travel."
"You mean a vehicle that can fly like a bird?"
"Something like that.
It doesn’t flap.
But it flies."
"Interesting." She turned the word over slowly, like she was tasting it.
"Interesting.
"You’re curious, aren’t you."
"I have been asleep for a very long time, cultivator.
Everything is interesting."
"Fair point."
"And you are going to retrieve it now.
This plane."
"That’s the plan."
Camilla laughed, the same low, delighted laugh she had produced when he had explained the same trick to her earlier in the cave.
It carried, this time, a slightly different quality.
There was more warmth in it.
More genuine appreciation.
The kind of amusement a person only produced when they had accepted, on some deep level, that they were going to enjoy the company of the person making them laugh for the foreseeable future.
She was filled with curiosity...
Stan didn’t mind her gaze as he willed the plane into existence.
The Bombardier materialized on a stretch of relatively flat, wind-packed snow perhaps fifty meters from where they stood.
Its polished fuselage caught the low polar sun in long mirror-bright reflections along its side.
Its landing gear settled into the compacted snow with the soft, muted crunch of thirty tons of engineered aircraft finding new solid ground.
The whole craft appeared in the polar air with the casual instantaneity that Stan was, slowly, becoming used to.
Camilla did not move for a long moment.
She stared.
Her red eyes tracked the length of the fuselage from nose to tail.
She catalogued the sweep of the wings.

She looked at the twin engines mounted at the rear, the raised T-tail, the small blinking navigation lights at the wingtips that had begun their patient rhythm the instant the aircraft had drawn breath in the real world.
"...This," she said slowly, "is your bird."
"This is my bird."
"It is enormous."
"It’s on the smaller end for its class."
"There is a larger class?"
"Yes, there is a much larger class."

chapters.title: Chapter 359: Into the Sky
paragraphs: Camilla was quiet for another moment.
"You do this often?" she asked.
"I’ve done it twice since I got it."
"Twice."
"The first time was when I abandoned it before impact. The second time is now."
She stared at the aircraft.
"You are going to be an interesting travel companion, cultivator."
"I get that a lot."

They walked toward the plane together. The wind buffeted them both. Camilla moved with the fluid, unhurried grace of a Royal Blood who did not feel the cold as an ordinary being felt it. Stan moved with the calm, focused efficiency of a man who was ready to be somewhere warmer.
He unlocked the aircraft. He extended the boarding stairs. He stepped aside and gestured her up.
She hesitated at the base of the steps. One long, pale hand rested on the aluminum railing. Her fingers pressed lightly against the cold metal.
"It is warmer inside?"
"Much warmer. Pressurized, temperature-controlled. It’ll feel like a room."
"A room that flies."
"That’s the general idea."
She climbed the steps and he followed.

The cabin was exactly as he had left it, the pressurized air still comfortable, the seats still upholstered, the small courtesy lighting still glowing gently in the corners. Whatever else the inventory did to objects it stored, it preserved them at a level of fidelity that made the transition feel like a magic trick even to someone who had done it twice.
Camilla stopped just inside the doorway.
She looked around.

She touched the leather headrest of the nearest seat with her fingertips. She ran a hand along the polished wood inlay of the cabin bulkhead. She looked up at the small overhead lights and down at the carpeted floor and along the row of small oval windows lined up on either side of the fuselage.
"This is a room," she said quietly. "You have installed a room inside your flying machine."
"That’s about right."
"For what purpose?"
"Comfort. Long flights. You’ll see."
She followed him toward the front.

He slid into the pilot’s seat. She settled into the co-pilot chair beside him with the careful, precise motion of a person who was not entirely sure what any of the surfaces around her were designed to do and was determined not to touch the wrong one.

Her red eyes tracked the cockpit with the same focused, cataloging attention she had applied to everything else. The control yokes. The throttles. The multi-display flight computer. The smaller auxiliary readouts that governed the various subsystems. The rows of small labeled switches on the overhead panel. The rudder pedals under Stan’s feet.
"This is your era’s version of an tamed beast, but you create a flying metal.bird that isn’t actually alive."
"More or less."
"It has many more instruments."
"Modern flight requires more information than gondola flight did."
"I would imagine."
She reached out. Her hand hovered over one of the throttle levers, not touching it, tracking the shape of it in the air.
"What does this do?"
"That controls the engines. Power output."
"And this?" She indicated the yoke.
"Steering. Pitch and roll."
"Pitch and roll."
"Which direction the nose points. Which way the wings tilt."
She was quiet for a moment.
"You understand all of this."
"I understand all of it."
"Instinctively?"
Stan considered.
"Something like that."

She let her hand drop back to her lap. She looked at him for a long, weighing moment, the way a Royal Blood looked at a mortal who kept doing things a mortal should not, by any reasonable measure, be able to do.
Then she smiled.
"Very well, cultivator. Fly your bird."

Stan ran the pre-flight checks with the calm, methodical rhythm of his installed pilot mastery. Every system reported nominal. The engines started smoothly, first the port, then the starboard. The turbines wound up to their idling speed with the familiar low hum of aviation-grade machinery, a sound that seemed to fill the cockpit and press outward against the small oval windows.
Camilla went very still.
Her head tilted slightly. Her red eyes narrowed at the instrument panel.
"That sound...
"The engines."
"It is inside the machine."
"It’s the machine breathing."
"Breathing."
"Something like that."
She listened for a long moment.
"...Acceptable."
Stan turned to her.
"Buckle in. Takeoff is going to be a little rough. This isn’t a runway."
Camilla arched an eyebrow. "Rough."
"For you? Probably not at all. For me? A little."
She smiled and reached for the seatbelt.

She examined it first, turned the buckle over in her fingers, tested the give of the strap, watched the way the metal tongue slid into the receiving latch when she pressed it in. The small click of the mechanism seemed to please her. She adjusted the shoulder harness with the same unhurried precision she seemed to apply to everything.
"Your era," she murmured, "loves its small clever objects."
"Toys, or small clever objects whatever you call them, keep us alive."
"So they do."
He rolled the aircraft forward on the snow.

The Bombardier’s takeoff performance was rated for prepared runways. It was capable of unprepared surfaces in emergencies, but the polar ice, wind-packed but uneven, with the subtle roughness of natural glacial terrain, was going to test the airframe’s tolerances in every possible direction.
Stan compensated.

His pilot mastery, drawing on the full range of adverse-condition takeoff procedures that had been installed in his mind, worked the throttles and the control surfaces in a continuous stream of small, precise corrections. The aircraft shuddered as it accelerated. The landing gear absorbed each impact with the compressed groan of a system operating at its outer limits. Stan felt the yoke fight him briefly as a crosswind gust tried to yaw the nose off the takeoff line.
He held the line.

He pushed the throttles further forward. The engines climbed from a hum into a roar. The airframe trembled around them. Loose snow blew up around the wheels in a fine white spray that the wind snatched away almost as fast as it appeared.

Beside him, Camilla’s hands settled loosely on the armrests. She did not grip. She did not brace. She simply watched, head slightly tilted, mouth slightly parted, red eyes moving between the horizon and the flickering readouts on the panel with the quiet fascination of a being who was, for the first time in a very long life, watching a mortal move a mountain of metal by pulling on a small stick.
He pulled back at the exact moment the aircraft’s ground speed crossed the minimum takeoff velocity.
The Bombardier lifted off.

chapters.title: Chapter 360: The Sky Between Two Eras
paragraphs: The rough shudder of the takeoff run vanished. The landing gear left the ice. The aircraft climbed smoothly into the polar air, its nose angled upward at a comfortable ten-degree pitch, its wings biting cleanly into the thin high-latitude atmosphere. The airframe steadied. The trembling stopped. The roar of the engines softened into a smooth, sustained thrum.
Stan let out a breath.
Beside him, Camilla was leaning slightly forward against her seatbelt, her red eyes fixed on the world falling away beneath them through the cockpit window.
She was smiling, she genuinely was...

The polar plain shrank below them. The compacted white terrain that had seemed endless from the ground revealed itself, from altitude, as a small pale wedge at the edge of a vast dark ocean. The horizon curved. The sky above deepened from pale blue into something richer.
"...I have not flown in a very long time," she said quietly. "Not like this."
"How did you fly, in the old era?"
"Cultivators of my rank flew directly. Through Qi manipulation. Without a construct. The wind supports the practitioner if the practitioner has sufficient comprehension of it."
"Faster than this?"

"Faster than a New Age airplane, yes. But not faster than this specific aircraft’s cruising speed for a sustained duration. Even Royal Bloods tire." She tapped the frame of the cockpit lightly with one long finger. "Whereas your machine simply carries you. Effortlessly. Endlessly. As long as the fuel holds."
"Fuel is easy to acquire."
"So I see."
She was quiet for a long moment. The polar landscape scrolled past beneath them.
"In the old era," she said, "flight was a mark of achievement. A practitioner who could ride the wind was a practitioner of considerable rank. The sky belonged to us. To cultivators. To the strong."
"And now?"
She gestured with one long finger at the world through the cockpit window.
"Now the sky belongs to whoever can afford a ticket."
Stan considered that.
"That’s one way to put it.

"It is not a criticism, cultivator. It is an observation. Your era has democratized what mine reserved for the mighty." Her red eyes tracked the wing outside the window. "There is something admirable in that. And something troubling."
"Which one wins?"
"I have not decided yet."
She turned her attention back to the window.
"But all these I just said are for those without tamed beast, after all one can easily ride a Flying QI beast to any location they want... You have a strange life, cultivator."
"I’ve been told."
He set the autopilot for Inksea and let the aircraft cruise.

The Antarctic interior fell away beneath them. The rough white terrain gave way to grey ocean. The elongated dusk of the polar latitudes gradually shifted into more ordinary daylight as they moved north. The engines hummed steadily. The cabin remained comfortable.

Camilla, in the seat beside him, watched the world scroll past through the window with the quiet, absorbing attention of a being who had emerged from decades of a constructed sky and was, for the first time in her lifetime, seeing a real one.
Stan let her look.

He busied himself with the small, ordinary business of flying, trim adjustments, altitude confirmations, the slow patient dance of transferring authority to the autopilot and confirming that the autopilot was, in fact, going to keep them in the air.

At cruising altitude, he tested the aircraft’s onboard satellite communications system. The polar interior had been a signal dead zone. As they crossed north into ordinary trans-oceanic airspace, the system reconnected to the global network with the small, cheerful chime of a device rejoining the world.
His phone lit up in his pocket.

Notification after notification stacked in rapid succession. Missed calls. Unread messages. News alerts. Snapchat pings. A voicemail from Sacha. Two voicemails from Maya. A blocked-number voicemail he could already guess the origin of.
The world, in the several days he had been away from it, had continued without him.
He sighed.
Camilla glanced over. "Trouble?"
"Just the world."
"Ah." She turned back to the window. "That one is always trouble."
Stan almost laughed.
He silenced the phone and slid it back into his pocket. Whatever the world wanted from him, it could wait until Inksea.
The Bombardier flew on.

The satellite chime faded and Stan looked out through the cockpit window at the world spooling past beneath them, grey ocean, thin cloud, the pale afternoon light of the middle latitudes, and did the calculation he had been quietly avoiding for the past hour.
The plane could not simply vanish on approach.

The last time he had willed the Bombardier back into the inventory, he had done it over open Antarctic ice with no witnesses within a thousand kilometers in any direction. A thirty-ton aircraft blinking out of existence a hundred meters above a private strip on Inksea Island was a different proposition. Air traffic control would notice. Coastal radar would notice. The half-dozen ground-crew on shift at any given hour would notice. Someone with a phone camera would notice.
Questions would follow. Stan was not in the mood for questions.
He tapped the comm panel awake and dialed the frequency for Inksea’s private aviation authority. The connection opened with the small cheerful blip of a modern tower answering a modern aircraft.
"Inksea Ground, this is Bombardier Global, inbound from the south, requesting priority approach and hangar accommodation for extended stay."

The voice on the other end was crisp, pleasant, unhurried. Stan gave a tail number. He gave a rough arrival window. He mentioned, in the practiced, unemphatic tone of a man who spent money the way other men spent breath, that expedited handling and discreet ground service would be appreciated and would be reflected accordingly on the invoice.
The voice on the other end became, if possible, even more pleasant. Approach was cleared inside of ninety seconds.
Camilla, in the seat beside him, watched the exchange with the small focused frown of a person cataloguing a new form of ritual etiquette.
"That was quick."
"Money is fast."
"It is?" Camilla’s brows furrowed, not getting the joke...
