chapters.title: Chapter 361: A Casual Miracle
paragraphs: ’I guess she doesn’t understand technology and money transfer...’ Seeing that Camilla didn’t get his joke, he shook his head and brought the Bombardier down through the cloud layer.

The polar mastery of the earlier takeoff was not needed here. Inksea’s private strip was a properly surfaced runway that ran along the north edge of the island, edged by low dune grass and the pale blue of the shallow coastal water. Stan set the aircraft on final approach with the calm, methodical grace of a pilot whose installed skill treated a paved runway as a courtesy the world had extended to him.
The landing gear touched down with a soft double chirp.
The airframe settled.
The reverse thrust engaged with a controlled roar, bled off the excess speed, and released. Stan taxied the aircraft off the active runway and onto the taxi line that ran parallel to the terminal.

A marshaller in a high-visibility vest was already waiting at the parking apron. He waved the illuminated batons in the practiced choreography of a professional guiding thirty tons of private aviation into a designated slot, nose forward, nose forward, gentle left, gentle right, hold. Stan followed the signals with the precise, unhurried attention of a man whose muscle memory had been paying attention to marshallers for years he had never actually lived.
The batons crossed above the marshaller’s head.
Stan set the parking brake.

He ran the shutdown sequence. Engines to idle. Fuel cutoff. Avionics to standby. The twin turbines wound down through a long descending hum until the cabin fell into the soft, high-altitude quiet of an aircraft that had, for the moment, finished being an aircraft.
He unbuckled. "We’re down."
Camilla unbuckled beside him with the same careful precision she had used to fasten the belt. She followed him back through the cabin to the door.
Stan pressed the small illuminated button on the interior bulkhead.

The cabin door unsealed with a soft hydraulic sigh. The boarding stairs unfolded outward and down, articulating on their servo joints with the smooth mechanical grace of a well-maintained system, and locked into place against the tarmac.
Camilla’s eyes tracked the entire motion. Her face did not change.

But Stan, who had by now spent enough time in her company to read the small shifts in the set of her mouth, caught the flicker of quiet appreciation that passed behind her red eyes. A door that opened itself. A stair that unfolded itself. A press of a single unlabeled button that caused thirty tons of engineered aircraft to arrange itself for its passengers.
She said nothing. He appreciated that.
They started down the stairs.
"Remember the deal," he said quietly.
She rolled her eyes. "Of course I will keep to the deal. I signed a blood contract, human. I am serious about this comradeship thing."
Stan smiled. "Good. And by the way, don’t worry about going back. I can return you to the realm whenever you feel like it."
Camilla’s eyes widened.
She stopped one step behind him. "...Really?"
Stan nodded, casually, as if he had just offered her a lift to a corner store.
Camilla did not move for a full second.

The blood contract they had sealed in the cave carried, among its several terms, one clause that could not be circumvented, neither party could lie to the other. There was no punishment for the attempt. There was only the sensation. A small, distinct pressure at the base of the skull that flared the instant a false statement was made, unmistakable to the bound party, impossible to fake and impossible to suppress.
She had felt nothing.
Which meant Stan was telling the truth.

Which meant that this man, this human, this cultivator whose apparent rank meant less and less each time she witnessed the impossible, could apparently traverse the boundary between realms as casually as he had just landed a metal bird on a stretch of paved ground.
A slow, considering glint appeared in her red eyes.
’Just as I thought. He truly is a hidden master. To move between realms so casually... what could a being of such standing possibly gain from concealing his strength?’
She followed him down the stairs without a word.
Stan, entirely unaware of the reappraisal happening behind him, reached the tarmac and turned to greet the small welcoming party waiting at the base of the airstair.
The VIP protocol officer stepped forward.

He was a neatly dressed man in his early forties, the pressed navy of Inksea’s private aviation authority uniform crisp against the sea breeze, a slim tablet tucked under one arm. His smile was the professional smile of a man whose job was to be pleasant to people who could afford to buy the terminal.

"Sir. Welcome to Inksea." He inclined his head. "Quite the skilled pilot, if I may say so. Based on your flight vector and the origin signal we picked up on approach, the aircraft appears to have come out of the Antarctic corridor. Flying through that region is not an easy thing."
Stan laughed it off with a small, dismissive wave. "Autopilot did most of the work."
The officer smiled the smile of a man who did not believe that for a second and was too professional to say so.
Beside Stan, Camilla’s mouth pulled into the faintest of pouts.

It was a small, almost imperceptible expression, the kind of thing that would have gone entirely unnoticed on a woman of ordinary presence. On Camilla Dragomir, it registered on the tarmac like a shift in the wind.

She wondered, briefly and with the small offended dignity of a nine-hundred-year-old Royal Blood, why the weak human in front of her had not for a single moment considered the possibility that she had flown the aircraft. Then she remembered that in this era women apparently did not fly metal birds by default, and she filed the observation away for later inspection of the era’s various assumptions.
The officer’s eyes flickered toward her once. Only once. He did not look again.

Whatever quality Camilla Dragomir carried in her presence, the quiet, unhurried authority of a being who had lived through years, vampires the man had only read and watch as fiction, the man didn’t know that this being in front of him was a vampire...
As a vampire cultivator, she isn’t affected by the sun as one would think...

chapters.title: Chapter 362: The Taste Of A New Era
paragraphs: As a vampire cultivator, Camilla isn’t affected by the sun as one would think...
Anyways, the officer’s professional instincts registered it immediately and correctly. His posture straightened by a fraction. His gaze fixed, respectfully and firmly, on Stan.
Stan noted it but said nothing.
"I’ll be leaving the aircraft here for a while," he told the officer. "Extended stay. Full-service hangar, standard security package, monthly maintenance rotation. Two months to start."
"Of course, Sir. If you’ll follow me to the main terminal, we can process the paperwork."

They walked. The tarmac shimmered gently in the afternoon light. The sea breeze off the coast carried the small clean smell of salt and jet fuel. Camilla walked at Stan’s shoulder with the fluid, unhurried grace of a woman who was, for the first time in her long life, walking across a modern airfield and finding it interesting.

The terminal was small, elegant, and quiet, the private aviation building of a coastal island that catered exclusively to the kind of client who required doors to open before they arrived at them. A receptionist behind a polished counter smiled as they entered. The officer led them past her and into a small conference room off the main lobby.
He set the tablet on the table and Stan sat.

Camilla remained standing behind him, one long pale hand resting lightly on the back of his chair, her red eyes tracking the small unfamiliar objects around the room with the quiet cataloguing attention she seemed to apply to everything in the modern world.
The paperwork rolled through in a series of small, efficient screens.
Aircraft parking fee. Hangar fee. Ground handling. Security detail. Scheduled maintenance rotation. Fuel reservation.
The itemized total scrolled to the bottom of the tablet and settled at a figure north of two hundred thousand dollars for the two-month arrangement.
Stan did not blink, instead he signed casually... At this point of his life money is nothing to him..

The officer processed the payment with the small unobtrusive grace of a man who had watched larger sums move across his tablet on quieter afternoons than this one. The screen chimed. The confirmation appeared. The officer stood.

"Everything is in order, Sir. Your aircraft will be moved to Hangar Six within the hour. If you require anything further during your stay, or if you would like us to prepare the aircraft for departure on short notice, please contact this line directly." He slid a small embossed card across the table. "I’ll personally handle any coordination."
Stan pocketed the card. "Appreciated."
He stood.

Two months was enough. Long enough to find a suitable stretch of coastal land somewhere quiet, long enough to build a private hangar and a modest strip of his own, long enough to arrange the small ordinary infrastructure that a man in his particular position now required. The Bombardier could sit here in the meantime and cost him nothing he would notice.
He turned to Camilla. "Ready?"
She inclined her head, the small, precise gesture of a Royal Blood granting assent.
"Lead on, Stan."

They left the conference room together. The receptionist smiled again as they crossed the lobby. The automatic doors slid open ahead of them with the soft mechanical whisper of a building that had been designed to remove every small friction from the lives of the people who walked through it.
The afternoon sun was warm on the pavement outside.
The sea breeze was gentle.
Stan stepped out into it, Camilla at his shoulder, and, for the first time in what felt like a very long several days, allowed himself the small, private thought that he was, finally, almost home.

The sea breeze off the coast was warm and salt-heavy. Stan stood on the pavement outside the terminal for a moment, letting it move over him, letting the small quiet fact of being back in the ordinary world settle in his bones.
Then his stomach reminded him, with the small unignorable insistence of a body that had finally noticed itself, that he had not eaten a proper meal in what was, by any honest measure, days.
"Before we do anything else," he said, "I need to eat."
Camilla glanced sideways at him.
"Cultivators do not require food."
"I know."
"Then why?
"Humans generally prefer not to starve when they have the option."
She considered that. "A reasonable preference."

Her red eyes lingered on him a beat longer than they needed to. It was the small, weighing look of a Royal Blood who had asked a question not to receive an answer but to see whether the answer would slip. She had watched him move mountains of engineered metal through the sky by pulling on a small stick. She had watched him hand over two hundred thousand dollars without a flicker. She had been waiting, quietly and patiently, for the seam in the disguise to show itself.
It had not shown itself.
He remained, for all outward appearances, a young man who was tired and hungry and wanted lunch.
She was, privately, becoming very entertained.
’Soon,’ she thought. ’Sooner or later he will let it slip.
"I packed food, actually," Stan added. "Before the whole Antarctica situation. Had it with me the whole time. But my head was too full to eat any of it."
"Understandable, given the circumstances."
"So. Somewhere with a table. And a chair. And a menu."
"Lead on."
They walked toward the small line of private cars idling at the terminal curb.
"Tell me, cultivator." Camilla’s voice was casual. Idly interested. The tone of a person making small conversation about the weather. "Is your era’s food truly so different from the food of mine?"
Stan considered the question as he opened the rear door of the waiting car for her.

"In your era, cultivators probably had spirit fruits. Qi rich mutant beast meat. Delicacies from spiritual regions. Ingredients that carried Qi and could nourish the body in ways that had nothing to do with taste."
"Yes."

"Almost none of that exists anymore. The spiritual beasts got teleported out too. With the lack of Qi, the spirit fruits stopped bearing. The regions that produced them lost their density. Whatever ordinary humans had access to in your time was probably very simple. Grains. Vegetables. Cooked meat. Salt if you were lucky."

chapters.title: Chapter 363: A Different Kind Of Strength
paragraphs: "Whatever humans had access to in your time was probably very simple. Grains. Vegetables. Cooked meat. Salt if you were lucky."
"That is a fair description, yes."
"Well. In the several thousand years since then, new age humans got very bored."
She looked at him. "Bored, huh?"

"Yes, bored. Without spirit fruits and cultivator delicacies to chase, humans spent thousands of years figuring out what to do with grains and vegetables and cooked meat. Every region on the planet developed its own methods. Every culture invented its own dishes. Sauces. Spices. Fermentation. Preservation. Techniques for cooking that don’t exist anywhere in nature and had to be invented from scratch. There are now, at conservative count, tens of thousands of distinct culinary traditions on the planet, and any decent-sized city will give you access to a hundred of them within a ten-minute drive."
Camilla was quiet. "...Tens of thousands."
"Give or take."
"For ordinary mortals."
"For anyone with a wallet."

She settled into the leather seat of the car and looked out through the window at the small clean streets of Inksea rolling past. To a vampire like her, whose eyes is mostly on blood, tens of thousands of different food was indeed a lot...
Stan slid in beside her letting her enjoy the sight...
The driver, a discreetly professional man in a dark suit provided by the airport’s VIP service, pulled smoothly away from the curb without a word.
"I would," Camilla said slowly, "like to sample this."
"That was the plan."
"A vampire’s palate is not as sensitive as a human’s, cultivator. Our taste for anything that is not blood is generally limited."
"Then we’ll find out what your exceptions are."
She almost smiled.

The car moved through Inksea with the quiet, unhurried competence of a professional driver on a familiar route. Stan let his shoulders finally, properly, unclench against the seat. The tension of the past several days had settled somewhere in the muscles of his back, and it was going to take more than a car ride to work it out, but the car ride was a start.
Beside him, Camilla watched the world roll past.
She was very quiet.

The vehicles on either side of them moved in smooth, patient traffic, sedans and small delivery vans and the occasional low sports car easing along the coastal road. The buildings rose on either side of the wider avenues in clean glass-and-concrete columns, catching the afternoon light in long angled reflections. The advertising screens along the sides of the taller structures scrolled through their patient, hypnotic loops of colour and text. Pedestrians moved along the walkways in their ordinary hundreds, going about their ordinary afternoons, walking dogs, carrying shopping, glancing at phones, laughing at friends.
Camilla watched all of it.
Her face did not change.

But her red eyes moved with the slow, cataloguing attention of a woman who had gone to sleep in a world of sects and kingdoms and had woken up in a world of glass towers and traffic lights, and was, in her own private and unhurried way, comparing the two.
’Did humanity truly grow weaker,’ she wondered, ’after Qi departed the world? Or did it simply grow strong along a different axis?’

The kingdoms and sects she remembered had been powerful in their own way. They had commanded mountains. They had reshaped landscapes. They had produced individuals who could level cities with a gesture. And yet, in all of those centuries, they had never produced this, the sheer, patient, distributed miracle of a coastal city on a random weekday afternoon, in which millions of ordinary people who could not lift a boulder had nonetheless collectively built glass towers and paved roads and mechanical carriages that moved without horses and glowing screens that displayed the faces of distant persons on command.
The tools were toys, from the perspective of a Royal Blood.
But there were so many of them. And every ordinary mortal had access to them. At least that’s what she thought...
She filed the thought away, unresolved, and returned her attention to the window.

Stan, glancing sideways at her, caught the small distant absorbed expression on her face and permitted himself a private smile. Introducing someone to the modern world was, apparently, becoming a recurring feature of his life. He was not sure how he felt about that.
The car pulled up outside a low, elegant building perched on the cliff edge of Inksea’s coastal promenade.

The restaurant was one Stan had used before, not the loudest or the most extravagant on the island, but the one with the best combination of quiet service, good food, and windows that overlooked the sea. He preferred restaurants where the waiters did not need to be told to leave him alone.

The maître d’ recognized him at the door and did not make a production of it. They were seated at a corner table by the tall glass windows, with the afternoon light coming in over the water in long slanted bars.

Camilla settled into her chair with the same fluid, unhurried grace she seemed to apply to every physical motion. She looked out through the window at the sea. She looked at the small unfamiliar objects on the table, the folded linen, the polished cutlery, the small candle in its glass holder. She picked up the menu.
She read it. For several minutes, she did nothing else.

Stan watched her read with quiet appreciation. She was not startled. She was not overwhelmed. She was simply, methodically, working through the list of dishes with the focused attention of a person trying to build an accurate mental map of a category she had not previously known existed.
"...There are eighty-four dishes on this menu," she said eventually.
"That’s about standard for a place like this."
"Eighty-four."
"Give or take."
"And this is one restaurant."
"One of hundreds on this island alone."
She lowered the menu slightly. Her red eyes met his over the top of the leather binder.
"When my ancestors spoke to me of the era that came after ours, cultivator, they described a world of weakened mortals scraping out existence in the ashes of what had once been our dominion."
"Uh-huh."
"They did not mention that the weakened mortals had, in the meantime, developed access to eighty-four distinct dishes per establishment."
"Ancestors tend to leave that part out."
Her mouth twitched at the corner. "So it seems."
Stan ordered.

And yet, in all of those centuries, they had never produced this, the sheer, patient, distributed miracle of a coastal city on a random weekday afternoon, in which millions of ordinary people who could not lift a boulder had nonetheless collectively built glass towers and paved roads and mechanical carriages that moved without horses and glowing screens that displayed the faces of distant persons on command.
The tools were toys, from the perspective of a Royal Blood.
But there were so many of them.
And every ordinary mortal had access to them.
At least that’s what she thought...
She filed the thought away, unresolved, and returned her attention to the window.
Stan, glancing sideways at her, caught the small distant absorbed expression on her face and permitted himself a private smile.
Introducing someone to the modern world was, apparently, becoming a recurring feature of his life.
He was not sure how he felt about that.
The car pulled up outside a low, elegant building perched on the cliff edge of Inksea’s coastal promenade.

The restaurant was one Stan had used before, not the loudest or the most extravagant on the island, but the one with the best combination of quiet service, good food, and windows that overlooked the sea.
He preferred restaurants where the waiters did not need to be told to leave him alone.
The maître d’ recognized him at the door and did not make a production of it.
They were seated at a corner table by the tall glass windows, with the afternoon light coming in over the water in long slanted bars.
Camilla settled into her chair with the same fluid, unhurried grace she seemed to apply to every physical motion.
She looked out through the window at the sea.
She looked at the small unfamiliar objects on the table, the folded linen, the polished cutlery, the small candle in its glass holder.
She picked up the menu.
She read it.
For several minutes, she did nothing else.
Stan watched her read with quiet appreciation.
She was not startled.
She was not overwhelmed.
She was simply, methodically, working through the list of dishes with the focused attention of a person trying to build an accurate mental map of a category she had not previously known existed.
"...There are eighty-four dishes on this menu," she said eventually.
"That’s about standard for a place like this."
"Eighty-four."
"Give or take."
"And this is one restaurant."
"One of hundreds on this island alone."
She lowered the menu slightly.
Her red eyes met his over the top of the leather binder.
"When my ancestors spoke to me of the era that came after ours, cultivator, they described a world of weakened mortals scraping out existence in the ashes of what had once been our dominion."
"Uh-huh."
"They did not mention that the weakened mortals had, in the meantime, developed access to eighty-four distinct dishes per establishment."
"Ancestors tend to leave that part out."
Her mouth twitched at the corner.
"So it seems."
Stan ordered.

chapters.title: Chapter 364: The Taste Of Civilization
paragraphs: Anyways Stan ordered widely; a spread of small plates from several different traditions rather than a single meal, on the theory that letting Camilla graze across the map would produce more information for her than a single deep dive into any one cuisine. Sashimi. A small tasting of dim sum. A cured meat and cheese board. A shellfish preparation the restaurant was known for. A pasta. A small piece of dry-aged steak. A trio of desserts to close.
The waiter took the order with the practiced neutrality of a man who had long ago stopped being surprised by anything a guest wanted to spend money on.
The food arrived in slow, elegant waves.
Camilla ate.

She did not exclaim. She did not gasp. She did not perform the small theatrical reactions of a person who had never encountered good food before. Her face remained, for the most part, its usual composed and unhurried Royal Blood mask.
But she tried everything.

She lifted each dish with careful, focused attention. She took small measured portions. She let each preparation settle on her palate for a considered moment before proceeding to the next. Her red eyes narrowed, once or twice, in the small precise expression of a being processing new information and finding some of it, quietly, surprising.
"The raw fish," she said at one point, of the sashimi. "This is not preserved."
"It’s fresh. Prepared this morning."
"It carries no seasoning to speak of."
"None. That’s the point. You taste the fish."
"...Interesting."
She tried the dim sum. The cured meats surprised her less than she had expected. The pasta was unlike anything she remembered from her era. Through it all, her expression changed little.

Stan, who had ordered enough for three people, watched with quiet amusement as the small elegant vampire across from him worked her methodical way through the entire spread without once acknowledging that she was doing so.
At one point, halfway through the pasta, she set down her fork and looked out through the window at the sea for a long moment.

"Ancestors of this world’s old era, my ancestors," she said quietly, "claimed dominion over the skies through cultivation. We commanded the wind. We reshaped mountains. We built palaces of Qi that no mortal hand could have raised, we carried that culture to new terra."
"Yeah."
"And yet, in my years of walking that world, I do not recall ever eating a meal like this one."
Stan set down his wine glass.
"That’s because no one in your era was bored enough to invent it.
"Explain."

"Cultivators had bigger problems than dinner. Ordinary mortals had bigger problems than dinner. Nobody in your era had the time, the resources, or the collective patience to spend three hundred years figuring out how to age beef in a temperature-controlled room so it would taste exactly like this. It took the modern world, with all its supposed weakness, to produce a civilization where enough people had enough spare time to obsess over how to cook a piece of meat correctly."
Camilla was quiet.
"That is," she said finally, "a strange thing to admire."
"Is it?"
"Humanity’s greatest talent, apparently, is the endless capacity to invent and to improve." She lifted her wine glass. "Even when the thing being improved is dinner."
"Especially when it’s dinner."
She almost laughed.
Stan smiled and lifted his own glass.
"Humans," he said, "are exceptionally talented at making things unnecessarily complicated. Food is one of the areas we’ve applied the talent most vigorously."
"So I see."
She sipped the wine.
The desserts arrived.

Camilla, who, up to this point, had maintained her characteristic composure with the discipline of a Royal Blood who did not intend to give a mortal the satisfaction of a strong reaction, encountered the second of the three desserts and went, for a brief unguarded moment, entirely still.

It was a small, delicate thing. A layered construction of dark chocolate and something cold and something warm, the flavours moving across the palate in slow overlapping waves. Stan had ordered it on a whim.
Camilla ate it with the small careful attention of a person trying not to notice that she was enjoying it.
She finished it.
She set the small silver spoon down.
She looked at the empty plate for a moment.
She lifted one long pale finger toward the passing waiter, and, without meeting Stan’s eyes, quietly requested another serving.
Stan said nothing.

He did not smile. He did not comment. He simply lifted his wine glass and took a very small, very careful sip, on the general principle that visibly noticing a Royal Blood’s small vulnerabilities was the kind of thing that shortened one’s lifespan.
Camilla’s red eyes flicked toward him once.
She said nothing.
But the small twitch at the corner of her mouth was, unmistakably, the expression of a woman who knew exactly what he was not saying and was choosing, for the moment, to permit it.
The second serving arrived.
She ate that one too.
They stepped out of the restaurant into the late afternoon light.

The sun was lower now. The sea beyond the cliff had gone from its bright noon blue into the deeper, softer blue of an afternoon sliding toward evening. The breeze was gentler. The pavement was warm underfoot.
Antarctica, Stan realized, already felt strangely distant.

The ice. The werewolves. The pact. The inheritance beneath the frozen mountain. All of it remained, waiting, exactly where they had left it. None of it had gone anywhere. But standing here on a warm coastal promenade with a full stomach and a nine-hundred-year-old vampire beside him quietly refusing to admit she had liked a chocolate dessert, the memory of the polar wind felt further away than it had any right to be.
He glanced sideways at Camilla.
She was looking out at the sea.
Her expression was, as ever, composed. Unhurried. Regal.
But there was something in the small quiet set of her mouth that was, he thought, faintly satisfied.
They started walking.

The promenade curved along the cliff edge in a long gentle arc. The afternoon light lay across it in long warm bars. In the distance, the small ordinary sounds of Inksea’s coastal traffic rose and fell in the patient rhythm of a city on an unhurried afternoon.

chapters.title: Chapter 365: The World Calls Back
paragraphs: Stan let his mind, finally, drift toward the small ordinary business of being home.
The messages waiting on his phone. The voicemails he had not returned. The missed calls he could already guess the origin of. The classes he had missed which he was due Zack had covered up for him...
The people who would want to know where he had been. The small, ordinary, unglamorous logistics of resuming a life that he had left behind several days ago on very short notice.

And, underneath all of that, the larger and less ordinary logistics of having brought home a Royal Blood vampire and now needing to figure out what, exactly, to do with her in a modern coastal city that had strong opinions about visas.
He glanced sideways at Camilla again.
She caught the glance and raised one dark eyebrow.
"Something on your mind, human?"
"Just wondering what kind of trouble I’ve walked back into."
"Ah."
"And what kind of trouble I’ve brought back with me."
Her red eyes glinted as she smiled slightly. "That, human, is entirely up to you."
Stan sighed. Deep down, past the good food and the warm afternoon light and the small satisfied quiet of a long journey nearly ended, he already knew the answer.

The inheritance beneath the ice was going to make its demands eventually. The pact with the Void Sovereign was going to make its demands. The world he had left behind several days ago was going to make its demands within the hour, as soon as he took his phone off silent.
But of all the storms currently gathering on the small crowded horizon of his life, the one he suspected was going to prove most consistently, most unpredictably, and most spectacularly troublesome,
was the elegant vampire walking beside him, watching the modern world scroll past for the first time, and quietly deciding what she thought of it.
He almost laughed. Instead, he tucked his hands in his pockets, matched her unhurried pace, and let the promenade carry them forward into the softening afternoon light.
Home, at last. Whatever home was going to mean now.
Waiting nearby, exactly where the airport staff had promised it would be, was the VIP sedan that had brought them here earlier that afternoon.

The sedan rolled up to the curb at the edge of the promenade with the near-silent glide of a well-maintained electric drivetrain, dark paint reflecting the coastal light in long liquid streaks along its flanks.
The driver stepped out. Opened the rear door. Said nothing.
Stan appreciated that.

Camilla settled into the leather seat with the same fluid grace she seemed to bring to every physical motion. She did not comment on the car. She did not comment on the driver. She simply arranged herself against the seat with the small unhurried dignity of a Royal Blood who had, by now, decided that surprise was undignified and refused to give the modern world the satisfaction of producing it in her.
Stan slid in beside her.
The door closed with the soft muted thump of a sealed cabin.
The sedan pulled smoothly away from the promenade and turned inland.
Inksea in the late afternoon was, Stan had always thought, at its best.

The coastal light lay across the island in long warm slants. The traffic thinned as the tourist crowds began their unhurried drift back toward hotels and rentals. The palms along the wider avenues stirred in the breeze with the small patient rhythm of well-watered trees on a well-planned island. The advertising screens on the taller buildings scrolled through their patient loops without the aggressive brightness they took on after dark.
Camilla watched all of it through the window.
She was, once again, very quiet.

But it was a different quiet than the one she had carried on the ride from the airport. Then, she had been cataloguing, building a first inventory of a world she did not know. Now, several hours and one long meal later, she was simply looking. The observation had softened into something closer to attention. She was letting the afternoon roll past her the way a person let a piece of music play through, not analysing every note, just permitting the whole to arrive.
Stan let her look. He took his phone out of his pocket.

He had silenced it back on the plane, when the satellite system had first reconnected to the global network and the small cheerful chime had been followed by the immediate cascade of notifications that the world had accumulated in his absence. He had not looked at it since. He had told himself, with the practical honesty of a man who knew his own tolerances, that he would deal with the world only after he had eaten.
He had eaten.
He unlocked the phone.

The notification stack was, if anything, worse than it had been on the plane. The satellite handoff had been the first wave. In the several hours since, the network had continued to catch up with itself, and the small red badge at the corner of the messaging app had climbed into a three-digit number that Stan chose not to look at too closely.
He scrolled to the top.

The list was in the usual rough order, missed calls at the top, then voicemails, then text threads sorted by most recent activity, then the various app notifications underneath. Snapchat. News. Two emails from the university. Something from the bank that was probably a fraud alert on the two-hundred-thousand-dollar hangar charge. A blocked-number voicemail he could already guess the origin of and did not intend to open.
His eyes moved down the list.
They stopped.

At the top of the text threads, above Maya, above Sarah, Sophie and the rest of his girls messages and calls to inquire about his well-being, above the university group chat, above every other name that had accumulated messages during his absence, was Sacha his sister...
Fourteen messages. Three missed calls. One voicemail.
Stan’s thumb hovered over the thread for a moment.

chapters.title: Chapter 366: The Deadline Nobody Followed
paragraphs: Fourteen messages. Three missed calls. One voicemail.
Stan’s thumb hovered over the thread for a moment.

Sacha was, at twenty-two, a person of very specific communicational economy. She said what she meant. She said it once. She did not chase her younger brother across a text thread unless something had happened that she had decided, on her own, warranted the chase.
Stan had told her before he left that he might be off-grid for up to ten days. She had accepted it and it had been three.

Which meant fourteen messages was not the volume of a worried sister. It was the volume of an older sister who had decided to worry, early, and on principle, and without waiting for the deadline to arrive. She had never thought that having her younger brother off the grid for a few days could make her this anxious.
Stan felt the small, familiar pull in his chest that only Sacha could produce.
He tapped the thread.
Sis Sacha: [Stan.]
[Hey. Just checking in.]
[Weekend? Oh, you’re already unreachable...]
[Not urgent. Wanted to talk about something.]
[Work time. Call me when you’re back on signal.]
[Day two. Still nothing.]
[I know you said ten. I’m still allowed to check.]
[I’m your older sister. I get to worry early.]
[Stan.]
[One word is fine.]
His thumb hovered over the reply field for a moment.

Beside him, Camilla shifted her weight in her seat, quiet as she watched the coastal light pass beyond the window. She said nothing. It was, he thought, one of her better qualities. She understood that silence, when offered at the right moment, could itself be a kindness.
He tapped the call icon.
The line did not finish ringing.
"Stan?" Her voice was small and tight all at once.
"I’m here," he said softly. "I’m okay."
A long, held breath escaped from the other end of the line.
"It’s only been three days."
"I know.
"I know I said I wouldn’t do this before ten."
"It’s understandable," Stan replied casually, a faint smile touching his lips. "You don’t have to explain yourself. I’d worry too if I was in your position."
His expression softened as he spoke.
Only he knew how true those words were.
If their positions had been reversed, he would’ve worried just as much, perhaps even more.

For a brief moment, he wondered what Sacha would think if she had seen him only a few hours ago. Pale and bloodied, barely standing, with his life hanging by a thread. What would Amelia think? Or Xenia? The girls would probably lose their minds if they ever saw him in such a condition.
Sacha, on the other hand, would probably fly halfway across the world just to hit him over the head before hugging him.
The thought made him chuckle inwardly.
Then his mind drifted back to the battle beneath the Antarctic ice.
The overwhelming pressure. The injuries. The taste of blood lingering in his mouth. And finally, the werewolves.
His eyes darkened almost imperceptibly.

Remembering their leader caused a familiar heat to stir within his chest. Rage boiled through him once more, cold and sharp. If circumstances had been even slightly different, things could have ended very badly that day.
Then, just as suddenly, the memory shifted.
He remembered Camilla standing before him.
He remembered watching her beat the absolute living shit out of the Werewolf leader with an expressionless face and all the casual brutality of someone disciplining an unruly child.
The image was so absurdly satisfying that his anger melted away almost immediately.
A smile slowly spread across his face.
’Payback is so sweet.’

He hadn’t even needed to lift a finger in the end. Gifting her things in exchange for her services while collecting rebates from the System was a brilliant arrangement, if he did say so himself. Everybody won. Well... everybody except the werewolf.
He was beginning to suspect that hiring an ancient vampire with expensive tastes to solve his problems might be one of the better investments he had ever made.

Still, watching Camilla enthusiastically beat the absolute living shit out of the Werewolf leader after he promised her the Spirit Pool was an oddly satisfying sight. The fact that she had done it for the promised payment hardly mattered in the end. The results spoke for themselves.
A small smile found its way onto his face.
’It was a worthwhile investment.’
He leaned back slightly in his seat, the smile lingering on his face.
He was home now. He was alive. His sister was worrying over him from half a world away, and beside him sat an ancient vampire who would happily tear a powerful werewolf apart for the right price.
Life was strange sometimes. He found that he didn’t particularly mind.

Anyways, Sacha was still on the phone. He listened as she exhaled, uneven, part relief, part the small embarrassed recognition of a person who had, in her own head, already lost the argument she had been rehearsing.
"Where are you?"
"On the way home from the airport. Just landed."
"Inksea?"
"Inksea."
"You came back early."
"Wrapped up faster than I thought."
A small pause followed.
"What did you want to talk to me about?" he asked, because he had not forgotten that she had started the thread with a reason.
"It can wait."
"Sacha."
"It can wait, Stan. Not a phone thing. A day or two."
"You sure?"
"I’m sure. Sleep. Eat. Call me tomorrow. And I mean actually call, not one of your two-word replies."
A small smile tugged at the corner of his lips.
"I will."
"Love you, bro."
"Love you too, sis."
The line went quiet.
He held the phone against his ear for a moment longer than the call required before finally lowering it. He didn’t put it away.
The others were waiting. Sacha was not the only person he had given the ten-day window to. She was merely the first to disregard it entirely. Somehow, that didn’t surprise him in the slightest.
He had a feeling she wouldn’t be the last.

After all, there were only so many people in his life willing to patiently wait ten days without hearing from him. Most of them had probably spent the last three wondering whether he was injured, unconscious, or simply being himself.
Knowing his luck, at least one of them had probably already prepared a lecture.
He suddenly wasn’t looking forward to checking the rest of his messages nearly as much as he had been a few minutes ago.

She said what she meant.
She said it once.
She did not chase her younger brother across a text thread unless something had happened that she had decided, on her own, warranted the chase.
Stan had told her before he left that he might be off-grid for up to ten days.
She had accepted it and it had been three.
Which meant fourteen messages was not the volume of a worried sister.
It was the volume of an older sister who had decided to worry, early, and on principle, and without waiting for the deadline to arrive.
She had never thought that having her younger brother off the grid for a few days could make her this anxious.
Stan felt the small, familiar pull in his chest that only Sacha could produce.
He tapped the thread.
Sis Sacha: [Stan.]
[Hey.
Just checking in.]
[Weekend?
Oh, you’re already unreachable...]
[Not urgent.
Wanted to talk about something.]
[Work time.
Call me when you’re back on signal.]
[Day two.
Still nothing.]
[I know you said ten.
I’m still allowed to check.]
[I’m your older sister.
I get to worry early.]
[Stan.]
[One word is fine.]
His thumb hovered over the reply field for a moment.
Beside him, Camilla shifted her weight in her seat, quiet as she watched the coastal light pass beyond the window.
She said nothing.
It was, he thought, one of her better qualities.
She understood that silence, when offered at the right moment, could itself be a kindness.
He tapped the call icon.
The line did not finish ringing.
"Stan?" Her voice was small and tight all at once.
"I’m here," he said softly.
"I’m okay."
A long, held breath escaped from the other end of the line.
"It’s only been three days."
"I know.
"I know I said I wouldn’t do this before ten."
"It’s understandable," Stan replied casually, a faint smile touching his lips.
"You don’t have to explain yourself.
I’d worry too if I was in your position."
His expression softened as he spoke.
Only he knew how true those words were.
If their positions had been reversed, he would’ve worried just as much, perhaps even more.
For a brief moment, he wondered what Sacha would think if she had seen him only a few hours ago.
Pale and bloodied, barely standing, with his life hanging by a thread.
What would Amelia think?
Or Xenia?
The girls would probably lose their minds if they ever saw him in such a condition.
Sacha, on the other hand, would probably fly halfway across the world just to hit him over the head before hugging him.
The thought made him chuckle inwardly.
Then his mind drifted back to the battle beneath the Antarctic ice.
The overwhelming pressure.
The injuries.
The taste of blood lingering in his mouth.
And finally, the werewolves.
His eyes darkened almost imperceptibly.
Remembering their leader caused a familiar heat to stir within his chest.
Rage boiled through him once more, cold and sharp.
If circumstances had been even slightly different, things could have ended very badly that day.
Then, just as suddenly, the memory shifted.
He remembered Camilla standing before him.
He remembered watching her beat the absolute living shit out of the Werewolf leader with an expressionless face and all the casual brutality of someone disciplining an unruly child.
The image was so absurdly satisfying that his anger melted away almost immediately.
A smile slowly spread across his face.
’Payback is so sweet.’
He hadn’t even needed to lift a finger in the end.
Gifting her things in exchange for her services while collecting rebates from the System was a brilliant arrangement, if he did say so himself.
Everybody won.
Well... everybody except the werewolf.
He was beginning to suspect that hiring an ancient vampire with expensive tastes to solve his problems might be one of the better investments he had ever made.
Still, watching Camilla enthusiastically beat the absolute living shit out of the Werewolf leader after he promised her the Spirit Pool was an oddly satisfying sight.
The fact that she had done it for the promised payment hardly mattered in the end.
The results spoke for themselves.
A small smile found its way onto his face.
’It was a worthwhile investment.’
He leaned back slightly in his seat, the smile lingering on his face.
He was home now.
He was alive.
His sister was worrying over him from half a world away, and beside him sat an ancient vampire who would happily tear a powerful werewolf apart for the right price.
Life was strange sometimes.
He found that he didn’t particularly mind.
Anyways, Sacha was still on the phone.
He listened as she exhaled, uneven, part relief, part the small embarrassed recognition of a person who had, in her own head, already lost the argument she had been rehearsing.
"Where are you?"
"On the way home from the airport.
Just landed."
"Inksea?"
"Inksea."
"You came back early."
"Wrapped up faster than I thought."
A small pause followed.
"What did you want to talk to me about?" he asked, because he had not forgotten that she had started the thread with a reason.
"It can wait."
"Sacha."
"It can wait, Stan.
Not a phone thing.
A day or two."
"You sure?"
"I’m sure.
Sleep.
Eat.
Call me tomorrow.
And I mean actually call, not one of your two-word replies."
A small smile tugged at the corner of his lips.
"I will."
"Love you, bro."
"Love you too, sis."
The line went quiet.
He held the phone against his ear for a moment longer than the call required before finally lowering it.
He didn’t put it away.
The others were waiting.
Sacha was not the only person he had given the ten-day window to.
She was merely the first to disregard it entirely.
Somehow, that didn’t surprise him in the slightest.
He had a feeling she wouldn’t be the last.
After all, there were only so many people in his life willing to patiently wait ten days without hearing from him.
Most of them had probably spent the last three wondering whether he was injured, unconscious, or simply being himself.
Knowing his luck, at least one of them had probably already prepared a lecture.
He suddenly wasn’t looking forward to checking the rest of his messages nearly as much as he had been a few minutes ago.

chapters.title: Chapter 367: Too Many Worried Hearts
paragraphs: With that, he scrolled through his messages and soon found Sophie’s DM. As if she had somehow sensed that he was online, she called him almost immediately.
He answered at once.
"STAN, you’re back!"
"Yes, I’m back. You don’t have to worry. I’m okay." He smiled softly as he replied.
"I know what I said. I said I would be fine. I said I would not check. I said I would trust the timeline. I have been lying to myself for seventy-two hours."
Underneath the heat there was a small, tight quaver, the sound of a young woman who had held herself together in public for three days and was, on a private line, finally permitting herself not to.
His expression softened slightly.
"I’m okay," he said gently. "On my way home now. Wrapped up early."
"You came back early."
"I came back early."
"...Good." A breath. "Your home, or mine?"
"Mine. First. I need a shower and about ten minutes with a wall."
That earned a faint snort of amusement from the other end of the line.
"Fine. Tomorrow."
"Tomorrow."
"I love you."
"I love you too."
Click. Beside him, the corner of Camilla’s mouth developed the faintest upward inclination. He elected not to comment on it.
Just like that he got his second call, it was from Maya...
"...Stan."
Quieter than Sophie. Steadier. The controlled composure of a young woman who had made a private decision not to spiral before the deadline and had, with visible effort, actually managed it.
"Hey."
"You’re back early."
"Yes."
"Good."
A small, measured breath echoed from the phone as he heard her continue... "I was doing very well, for the record. I had seven more days budgeted. I was going to be very impressive about it..."
A faint smile appeared on his face.
"I believe you. I had a whole speech prepared for day eleven, in case you were late."
"You can still give it to me."
"No." A wry, tired exhale escaped her. "A day-eleven speech doesn’t work on day three. Wrong energy."
"That checks out."
"Come see me. Not tonight. When your head is on straight, or wait, I’ll make up time to give you a surprise visit later..."
"I will." A small pause settled comfortably between them before she spoke again.
"...I missed you.
The smile on his face softened slightly. "I missed you too."
"Stay safe for me, Stan. Welcome back from your business that made you unreachable for three days... I love you..."
Click
The call ended on that note, and his gaze moved to the next name on the list.
’Mia.’ He hesitated for a single beat before tapping her name.
Mia was, of all the names waiting in the stack, the one who worried him most on this kind of call, not because she would be angry, but because she wouldn’t be.
She never was. He called her, and unlike the former two, she seemed to be a little busy. After two rings, she picked up.
"Stan?"

Small. Not sharp, like Sacha. Not blazing, like Sophie. Not composed, like Maya. Just, small. The voice of a girl who had spent three days telling herself she had no right to feel the tight thing in her chest because he had said ten, and three was well inside ten, and being worried already was being unreasonable.
"Hey. It’s me. I’m okay. Wrapped up early."
A very small, very sharp intake of breath. Then silence.
Not the silence of a person who had run out of words. The silence of a person who had suddenly, entirely, forgotten she had been holding her breath.
"Mia."
"...I’m here."
"You didn’t message. I looked."
"I didn’t want to be the one who..." She stopped herself before starting again, softer this time. "You said ten. I was trying to be good."
Something in his chest went quietly sideways.
"You don’t have to be good, Mia. You can just message me."
"...Okay."
"I’ll come see you soon. Give me a day or two."
"Okay."
"You don’t have to say okay to everything."
"...okay, I’m sorry my love." He almost laughed.
She laughed, blushing on the other end of the line, the small, breathy exhale of a girl who had heard his reply and was choosing to be embarrassed rather than upset.
"Come soon."
"Promise."
Click
He rested the phone against his knee for a moment and drew a slow breath.
The faint upward curve at the corner of Camilla’s mouth had settled into something closer to private amusement.
"You seem to have quite the harem," she observed idly. "They all sound rather concerned for you."
Her crimson eyes flickered briefly toward the phone in his hand before continuing.
"I do wonder what strange equipment that is. It allows you to communicate with all of them across such great distances without the slightest trace of Qi. Humans truly are strange creatures."
Her lips curved ever so slightly. "And busy ones, apparently."
Stan glanced at the remaining names waiting for him on the screen before letting out a quiet breath.
"I’m about to become much busier."
He wasn’t about to explain to her that having a harem of girls is not quite the common thing amongst new age humans...
The next was Sarah. Two rings, and she did not say hello.
"Stan."
He winced. "Hey."
"You said up to ten days."
"I did."
"It has been three."
"It has."
"Do you know how many times I’ve checked my phone today?"
"...How many?"
"Enough that my phone probably thinks we’re dating, Stan." He laughed softly at that.
Then her voice softened just a little.

"And before you ask, no, I wasn’t worried. I was merely considering all the perfectly reasonable explanations for why you disappeared. Alien abduction. Kidnapping. Falling off a cliff. Being eaten by a bear."
"What if they were bears?"
A brief silence greeted his words before Sarah spoke again.
"Tell me you’re joking."
"I’m not."
Stan laughed it off lightly.
Hearing his laugh, Sarah became even more convinced that he was simply toying with her.
"Your life is a serious matter, Stan. It’s not something to joke about."
"Okay, Sarah." He replied knowing fully well that it’d be hard for her to believe him if he told her that he had slain a polar bear a few hours ago

Anyways, the bright, brisk indignation lasted only a moment before it softened into something quieter, the shift Sarah always made when she permitted herself to let the gentler version underneath show through.
"Are you actually okay?"
"I’m okay. Wrapped up early."
A small pause followed.
"And you’re going to rest when you get home, right? Not immediately throw yourself into whatever ridiculous thing you’ve decided to do next?"
"...Probably."
"Stan."
"I’m resting."
"Good. Want me to come over tomorrow?"
He could hear the anticipation and eagerness in that voice...

chapters.title: Chapter 368: Welcome Back, My Hero
paragraphs: "Good. Want me to come over tomorrow?" She asked softly...
He could hear the anticipation and eagerness in that voice. His chest did the same small, quiet turn it had done for Mia.
"I’d like that."
Truthfully, he wasn’t opposed to all of them coming tomorrow.
In fact, it might be better that way.

The secret had already outlived its usefulness. Maya and Sophie knew about each other now, and neither had set anything on fire. He still wasn’t entirely sure how that miracle had occurred, but he wasn’t inclined to question it too closely.
The others, however, were still in the dark.
Sooner or later, that conversation was going to happen.
Preferably sooner. Better to face the storm head-on than let it gather strength in the distance.
Hopefully, they would take it as well as Maya and Sophie had.
’Hopefully.’
"...Good. Don’t die on the way." He heard her say teasingly
"I won’t."
"Love you, idiot."
"Love you."
~Click~ the call ended...
’Three more names left.’ Stan sighed

Camilla glanced at him before saying softly, "So new age humans are so weak that even a non-mutant bear is considered frightening. I suppose the strength they derive from those shooting toys will always remain borrowed strength. No matter what they create, it is not true strength."

Stan was silent for a moment. He thought of the mechas humanity had already begun to develop. They were still in their infancy, but some of the prototypes were already capable of feats that would have seemed impossible only decades ago.
And yet, he found himself unable to disagree with her.
Even if an ordinary human piloted a machine powerful enough to shatter mountains, that power would still belong to the machine. Strip it away, and they would remain ordinary.
It was strength that could be wielded, not strength that could truly be called one’s own.
In that regard, Camilla was right.
The difference between cultivation and technology had never merely been one of power. It was one of ownership. He sighed softly.
Humanity’s path was different from that of cultivators. Whether one was superior to the other remained to be seen.
’Amelia.’ He looked at the name on his screen before giving her a call.

While their relationship was still formal by most standards, Stan was interested in her, and he knew she felt the same way. There was also the matter of the investigation into those impersonating his Sir Streak TikTuk alias that he wanted an update on.

He tapped the call icon. The line did not ring. It picked up before the first ring had even completed, the immediate crispness of a call intercepted by a person whose phone had already been in her hand.
"Stan." The voice that came was very controlled.

That was what caught him. Amelia did not do controlled. Amelia did composed, the unhurried self-possession of a woman who owned significant shares in a major film studio and had spent a lifetime being the most collected person in every room she walked into. Controlled was the tool she reached for when composed had failed.
"Hey," he said gently.
One very small breath echoed through the phone as she said, "You are alive."
"Yeah."
"You are in Inksea."
"Yes, just landed."
"You are unharmed."
He hesitated for the briefest of moments before replying. "Yes I’m unharmed."

Another small breath. Then the smallest possible crack in the controlled surface, the softer, warmer voice that only ever appeared on private phone lines, and had, over the past several weeks, been appearing more and more often.
"...Good."
He waited then said softly, "Amelia."
"I am processing."
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his lips. "Take your time."
"You said up to ten days, Stan."
"I did."
"It has been three."
"I know."
"Vanguard has been on a readiness posture for seventy-two hours."
"...A readiness posture?"
"At my instruction. We have multiple leads, but nothing substantial yet."
He closed his eyes for a moment. "That’s a little early."
"I am aware.

A small pause followed. Then the controlled surface finally cracked entirely, giving way to the softer, warmer voice that only ever appeared on private phone lines and had, over the past several weeks, been appearing more and more often.
"...I sent a lot of messages. I know it has only been three days, Stan. I know you said ten. I simply could not help it."
"I know."
"Do not think less of me for it."
"Amelia," he said softly, "there isn’t a world where I would."
Silence greeted his words for several long seconds.
Then, very quietly, so quietly he almost missed it,
"...Welcome back, my hero." She said in a meek shy voice and then...
Click
The call ended, Stan could feel that she was embarrassed...
Meanwhile at the other end of the line, Amelia remained seated in silence in a room long after the call had ended.
She sat rigidly upright in the high-backed office chair, the tailored lines of her charcoal-grey power suit still perfectly pressed despite the long day.
The fitted jacket hugged the full, heavy curve of her bust, the silk blouse beneath strained just slightly across the deep cleavage that the low V-neck deliberately framed.
A narrow pencil skirt clung to the generous flare of her hips and the soft thickness of her thighs, the fabric stretched taut where it met the edge of the seat.

Even in the dim light of the office that evening, it’s evening at her place because of the the different time line, despite the dim light, the mature, sensual weight of her body was unmistakable, the kind of lush, lived-in fullness that belonged to a Mild...
Slowly, she closed her eyes and pressed the phone gently against her chest as the tension she had been holding onto for the past seventy-two hours quietly left her body.
’He is alive. He is home. He is safe.’
Somehow, those three facts alone felt enough to make the rest of the world seem a little less important. The corners of her lips curved into a small, helpless smile.
As their conversation replayed in her mind, something clicked almost immediately, another problem presented itself.
’Does this mean he’s interested in me now?’ Her eyes slowly opened before narrowing ever so slightly. ’He has to be... right?’

She wasn’t normally this uncertain. Amelia Don had spent her entire life making difficult decisions with absolute confidence. Multi-million dollar investments were easier than this. Negotiating with powerful businessmen was easier than this.
This, however, was terrifying.
’Should I send him an "I love you" message?’ Her fingers unconsciously tightened around her phone.
’No. That’s still far too sudden. ...Or is this the perfect moment? No, it’s a bad idea, he literally just came back’

The call ended, Stan could feel that she was embarrassed...
Meanwhile at the other end of the line, Amelia remained seated in silence in a room long after the call had ended.
She sat rigidly upright in the high-backed office chair, the tailored lines of her charcoal-grey power suit still perfectly pressed despite the long day.
The fitted jacket hugged the full, heavy curve of her bust, the silk blouse beneath strained just slightly across the deep cleavage that the low V-neck deliberately framed.
A narrow pencil skirt clung to the generous flare of her hips and the soft thickness of her thighs, the fabric stretched taut where it met the edge of the seat.

Even in the dim light of the office that evening, it’s evening at her place because of the the different time line, despite the dim light, the mature, sensual weight of her body was unmistakable, the kind of lush, lived-in fullness that belonged to a Mild...
Slowly, she closed her eyes and pressed the phone gently against her chest as the tension she had been holding onto for the past seventy-two hours quietly left her body.
’He is alive.
He is home.
He is safe.’
Somehow, those three facts alone felt enough to make the rest of the world seem a little less important.
The corners of her lips curved into a small, helpless smile.
As their conversation replayed in her mind, something clicked almost immediately, another problem presented itself.
’Does this mean he’s interested in me now?’ Her eyes slowly opened before narrowing ever so slightly. ’He has to be... right?’
She wasn’t normally this uncertain.
Amelia Don had spent her entire life making difficult decisions with absolute confidence.
Multi-million dollar investments were easier than this.
Negotiating with powerful businessmen was easier than this.
This, however, was terrifying.
’Should I send him an "I love you" message?’ Her fingers unconsciously tightened around her phone.
’No.
That’s still far too sudden. ...Or is this the perfect moment?
No, it’s a bad idea, he literally just came back’

chapters.title: Chapter 369: Home, At Last
paragraphs: ’Should I send him an "I love you" message?’ Her fingers unconsciously tightened around her phone.
’No. That’s still far too sudden. ...Or is this the perfect moment? No, it’s a bad idea, he literally just came back’

Even though he had called her immediately after landing. Even though he had reassured her without hesitation when she admitted she couldn’t stop herself from worrying about him. Even though he hadn’t thought less of her for it. She still felt a bit afraid that she’ll blow everything...
But what if it really was the perfect moment. Wasn’t this exactly the sort of moment people confessed their feelings in romance films?
Then again, romance films also had an alarming tendency to make terrible life decisions seem profound.
Amelia was suddenly beginning to suspect she had spent far too much time investing in one, the past few days after Stan changed her view in men...
’No. No, absolutely not. I am not taking romantic advice from cinema.’
She buried her face in her hands for several long seconds before peeking at her phone once more.
’What if I blow it?’ That thought, more than anything else, gave her pause.
For the first time in a very long time, Amelia found herself wanting something enough to become afraid of losing it before she’d ever had it.
She wasn’t in a hurry. She could wait. ...Probably.
Her thumb hovered uncertainly over the message icon for several seconds before retreating altogether.
’No. Absolutely not.’ She pressed the phone against her chest once more and allowed herself a small smile.

’Welcome back, my hero,’ she thought quietly. ’Take your time. I’ll wait. No I shouldn’t wait, what if someone takes him from me, I should think about it carefully and send him a message by night time...’

Meanwhile, Stan sat very still for a moment. He checked up on Xenia as well, it’s been long, then after that he sent Vivian a message, asking how both the company and her family had been during the days he was away.
He lingered for a moment after sending it, staring at the darkened screen before finally setting the phone face-down on his thigh.
Beside him, Camilla, who had, through all six calls, maintained the small, courteous fiction of not listening, finally turned her head fully towards him.
The warm coastal light fell softly across her profile. Her crimson eyes had softened in the afternoon glow into something closer to deep, clear garnets.
She looked at him for a long, weighing moment.
Then, in the small, unhurried tone of a woman offering a completely neutral observation:
"Human."
"Yeah?"
"You told them ten days."
"I did."
"And returned in three."
"I did."
"And every one of them had already begun to worry."
"...Yeah."
"Some of them sound as though they consider you theirs.
"I’ve noticed that too."
"And you permit this."
"I permit a lot of things."
The corner of her mouth curved faintly.
"I am going to enjoy watching this play out," she said softly. "Three days. Ten days. Such a short span of time, and they worry as though decades have passed. Humans truly are fascinating creatures."
Her crimson eyes shifted briefly towards him.
"Affection makes all of you remarkably unreasonable."
Stan laughed softly. "I was afraid you were going to say that."
She didn’t even know he had his eyes on her as well. Somehow, he had a feeling she would prove no different when her turn came.
Camilla merely turned her face back towards the window, the afternoon light painting her pale features in soft gold as the coastal scenery slipped quietly by.
Stan let out a slow breath, tucked the phone into his pocket, and let his head rest, just for a moment, against the back of the seat.
The sedan rolled on.
The coastal road curved gently inland. The palms passed. The soft warm light of the late afternoon lay across the dashboard in long slanted bars.
Home at last.

The sedan turned off the coastal road onto the smaller inland avenue that led toward Stan’s building. The palms thinned. The light shifted subtly as the road climbed in a gentle rise along the back of the island toward the quiet residential quarter where Stan had, several months and what felt like several lifetimes ago, quietly acquired a penthouse.
Home. It was strange, he thought, how unfamiliar that word felt after only three days.

Camilla, seated beside him, watched the streets outside narrow into the small, clean grid of an affluent residential district. Her eyes lingered briefly on the understated architecture and immaculate landscaping that spoke less of ostentation than of old money and deliberate privacy.
"You live here."
"I do."
"Alone?"
"Yes."
She considered that for a moment before replying.
"That will change, temporarily."
"So I gathered."
The faintest hint of amusement touched her expression.
"I wonder what your harem would think when they see me?"
Stan laughed softly under his breath.
"Probably depends which one sees you first."
That earned him the ghost of a smile.

The sedan slowed before finally pulling up outside a tall pale-stone building set back slightly from the street. Its lower floors were half-hidden behind carefully shaped hedges and flowering shrubs, while its upper levels rose into the warm afternoon sky with the quiet, unadvertised expense of a residence that had never needed to announce itself. There were no garish displays of wealth or excessive ornamentation, simply understated luxury and the sort of discretion that wealth often purchased when it no longer needed to impress anyone.

The sedan slowed before finally pulling up outside the building. By the time it came to a stop, the driver was already reaching for his door, moving with practised efficiency to open the rear door for them.
Stan stepped out first, taking in the familiar sight of the building before him. For the first time since Antarctica, something inside him finally began to settle.
’Home sweet home.’
Camilla followed him from the sedan with the fluid, unhurried grace she seemed to bring to everything she did. She straightened once her heels touched the pavement and paused for a moment in silence.

Her crimson eyes travelled upward over the pale-stone façade of the building before settling upon the small polished brass plate mounted discreetly beside the entrance, the building’s name engraved upon it in elegant, understated script.
There was no surprise upon her face. Only quiet observation.
Then she turned her head ever so slightly toward Stan, one dark eyebrow arching delicately.
"Stan."
"Yeah?"
"You appear to be quietly wealthy."
"I appear to be, yes."
"Ah, well it’s to be expected since you give spirit pools out like candies."
The single syllable carried an extraordinary amount of meaning despite revealing absolutely none of it.
She was silent for another moment before adding thoughtfully,
"You have a curious habit of concealing things."
"Do I?"
"You concealed your cultivation. You concealed your abilities. You concealed your resources. Apparently, you also conceal your money. I’m curious about the real you..."
Stan considered that briefly. "When you put it that way, it sounds worse than it is."
"It sounds exactly as it is."
He found he couldn’t argue with that. She can think whatever she wants he won’t correct her, that’s his only leverage.
Without another word, she stepped past him and made her way toward the entrance as though she had already decided she approved of it.
Stan moved ahead of her and pushed open the gate entrance door and stepped inside with her...
He tucked his phone back into his pocket, drew a small quiet breath, and followed after her.
’Home. At last.’

chapters.title: Chapter 370: A Quiet Resolve
paragraphs: They entered through the gate... The lobby was quiet in the late afternoon.
Stan walked in, and Camilla followed half a step behind him.

She was, once again, very quiet. Her red eyes moved across the lobby with the small unhurried cataloguing attention she had brought to every new interior since Inksea International, the recessed lighting, the soft ambient music laid so low it barely registered as sound, the arrangement of low couches around a slim brass sculpture that served no obvious function beyond looking expensive. She did not comment.
She did, however, tilt her head very slightly at the sculpture.
Stan almost smiled.
The elevator was at the far end of the lobby. Stan tapped his phone against the reader. The doors slid open onto a mirrored interior. He stepped in. Camilla followed.
The doors closed.

The elevator began, silently, to rise. Camilla looked at her own reflection in the mirrored panel opposite. She looked at the small illuminated numbers above the door counting upward. She looked at Stan.
"Human."
"Yeah."
"This box is climbing."
"It is."
"How."
"Motors. Cables. Counterweights. Same principles as any lift you would have seen in the old era, just quieter and faster and better balanced."

She was quiet for the rest of the ride. Through her spirit sense, she directly observed the intricate mechanisms hidden within the walls of the elevator and understood their workings almost immediately.
The elevator arrived at the top with the small chime.

The doors opened directly into a small private vestibule, no shared hallway, no other doors, just a single dark wooden entrance framed by two low potted trees and a discreet keypad panel set into the wall beside it.
Stan tapped his phone against the reader. The door unlocked with a soft mechanical click and he pushed it open.
The penthouse opened out in front of them.

Late afternoon light poured in through the tall floor-to-ceiling glass along the far wall, laid across the pale wood of the floor in long warm bars. The main living space stretched out low and wide and quiet, a long sectional sofa arranged around a low stone coffee table, an open kitchen along one side with a marble island and a row of hanging brass pendants, a dining table set for six that had never actually seated six, and beyond all of it the wide sliding glass that opened onto the wraparound terrace and the long unobstructed view of the sea.
Camilla stepped inside. She stopped one pace past the threshold.
She looked at the ceiling. She looked at the floor. She looked at the long soft line of the sofa. She looked at the marble island. She looked at the pendants and then looked at the view...
She was very still as Stan closed the door behind them.

He set his keys in the small tray on the console by the entrance. He toed off his shoes and stepped out of them with the small grateful sigh of a man who had been in the same pair for what was, by any honest measure, days. He padded past her toward the living space.

"Make yourself comfortable. Kitchen’s open. Fridge has whatever’s still edible. Terrace is through the sliders. Guest bathroom is the second door on the left down that hall. There’s more, actually, I’ll show you the rest properly in a minute. I need a shower first."
Camilla did not answer immediately.
She was still, very quietly, looking at the view.

"... Your place is nice..." she complimented and went quiet for another moment. Then she turned her head slowly toward him, one dark eyebrow arched as she noticed the small corner of his mouth curving with private amusement. He shrugged her compliment off...
"Shower," he said. "Ten minutes. Then I’ll show you around properly."
She inclined her head, the small, precise gesture of a Royal Blood granting permission to a mortal who did not, technically, require it, and turned her attention back to the view.
Stan closed the door to the master bedroom behind him and allowed himself a quiet breath of relief.
Home.
He hadn’t realized just how much he had missed the simple comfort of his own space until now.
The bathroom was, in Stan’s opinion, one of the best rooms in the penthouse. It had been quite some time since he bought the apartment, but its design had never ceased to amaze him.

He had not designed it. He had bought the place fully finished, and whoever had specified the fixtures had done so with the small, expensive care of a person who understood that a bathroom, properly considered, was one of the two rooms in a home where a person spent time alone with themselves and their thoughts, and that both of those rooms deserved to be beautiful.

The room was long and low, done in warm pale stone, with a deep freestanding tub against one wall and, his preferred feature, a walk-in shower behind a single frameless glass panel along the other, with a broad overhead rainhead and a second handheld unit on a sliding rail and a small niche cut into the stone for whatever bottles a person kept in a shower. ... Stan stripped out of his clothes with the slow, tired efficiency of a man whose body had, over the past several days, endured far more than it had ever asked for.
He caught his reflection in the mirror and paused.

The Bone-Tempering Pill and the Jade Purity Elixir had, at some point during the past week, quietly completed their work on his body. The damage he had suffered at the hands of the Werewolves should have left behind a lifetime of reminders, but thanks to the lifesaving pill he had purchased from the System Shop, everything had healed without leaving so much as a scar. He was as good as new.
His gaze slowly lowered to his stomach, and he unconsciously touched the spot where there had once been nothing but torn flesh and blood.
He sighed softly.
"It’s hard to believe there was once a gaping hole in my stomach," he murmured to himself. "My skin was practically scraped off too. I was a bloody mess back then."

He could still remember it vividly. The overwhelming pain. The sensation of his consciousness fading as death slowly reached out for him. The smell of blood that refused to leave his senses for days afterward.
There had been a moment when he genuinely thought he was going to die in Antarctica.
Thankfully, the System Shop had possessed the one thing capable of dragging him back from death’s doorstep.
His expression darkened slightly as memories of the Werewolves surfaced in his mind.
"Those bastard Werewolves..." he muttered coldly. "It’s only fitting they paid with their lives."
His eyes narrowed faintly.
"Especially that fucking bastard of a leader."

He didn’t pity them in the slightest. They had hunted him without hesitation, intending to tear him apart and leave his corpse buried beneath Antarctica’s endless ice. Had their positions been reversed, they wouldn’t have shown him even the slightest mercy.

The only thing he regretted was that he hadn’t been the one to kill every last one of them himself. In the end all he needed was strength, so that if such a scenario was to repeat itself, he wouldn’t be so helpless next time...
Antarctica had taught him many things. Strength was one of them.
Next time, he intended to be strong enough that survival wouldn’t need to depend upon luck or the contents of the System Shop.
